chapters.title: Dedication: To Lorenzo de' Medici
paragraphs: To the Magnificent Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici

Those who wish to win a prince's favor customarily come before him with whatever they hold most precious, or whatever they see him take most delight in. So one often sees princes presented with horses, arms, cloth of gold, precious stones, and similar ornaments worthy of their greatness.

Wishing, then, to present myself to Your Magnificence with some testimony of my devotion, I have found nothing among my possessions that I hold dearer or value more than my knowledge of the actions of great men — acquired through long experience of contemporary affairs and continual study of antiquity. I have reflected on this knowledge with great and prolonged diligence, and now send it, condensed into a small volume, to Your Magnificence.

Although I may consider this work unworthy of your notice, I trust in your kindness that it will nevertheless be acceptable, since I cannot make a better gift than to offer you the chance to understand in the shortest time all that I have learned in so many years and through so many troubles and dangers. I have not embellished this work with swelling or magnificent phrases, nor stuffed it with rounded periods or any other extrinsic allurements or adornments with which so many writers decorate their works. I wished either that it should receive no honor at all, or that the truth of the matter and the weight of the theme alone should make it acceptable.

Nor do I hold with those who consider it presumption for a man of low and humble condition to dare to discuss and settle the concerns of princes. Just as those who draw landscapes place themselves below in the plain to contemplate the nature of mountains and high places, and climb the high mountains to contemplate the plains, so to understand the nature of the people it takes a prince, and to understand that of princes it takes one of the people.

Take, then, Your Magnificence, this small gift in the spirit in which I send it. If you read and consider it with diligence, you will see my extreme desire that you attain the greatness that fortune and your other qualities promise. And if Your Magnificence, from the summit of your greatness, will sometimes turn your eyes to these lower regions, you will see how undeservedly I suffer a great and continual malignity of fortune.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — How Many Kinds of Principalities There Are
paragraphs: All states, all powers that have held and hold rule over men, have been and are either republics or principalities.
Principalities are either hereditary, with a long-established family on the throne, or they are new.

The new ones are either entirely new — as Milan was to Francesco Sforza — or they are, as it were, members annexed to the hereditary state of the prince who has acquired them, as the Kingdom of Naples was to that of the King of Spain.

Such acquired dominions are either accustomed to live under a prince or to live in freedom; and they are acquired either by the arms of the prince himself, by the arms of others, by fortune, or by ability.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Hereditary Principalities
paragraphs: I will leave aside all discussion of republics, since I have written of them at length elsewhere, and will address only principalities. I will keep to the order indicated above, and discuss how such principalities are to be ruled and preserved.

I say at once that hereditary states, long accustomed to the family of their prince, are less difficult to hold than new ones. For a prince of average powers need only not transgress the customs of his ancestors, and deal prudently with circumstances as they arise, to maintain himself in his state — unless some extraordinary and excessive force deprives him of it. And if he is so deprived, whenever anything goes wrong for the usurper, he will regain it.

In Italy, for example, we have the Duke of Ferrara, who could not have withstood the attacks of the Venetians in '84, nor those of Pope Julius in '10, had he not been long established in his dominions. The hereditary prince has less cause and less need to give offense; he will therefore be more loved; and unless extraordinary vices cause him to be hated, it is reasonable that his subjects will be naturally well disposed toward him. In the antiquity and duration of his rule, the memories and motives for change are lost; one change always leaves a foothold for the next.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Mixed Principalities
paragraphs: The difficulties come with a new principality. First, if it is not entirely new but is, as it were, a member of a composite state, the changes arise chiefly from an inherent difficulty in all new principalities: men willingly change their rulers, hoping to better themselves, and this hope leads them to take up arms against the current ruler. In this they are deceived, finding by experience that they have gone from bad to worse. This follows also from another natural and common necessity, which always forces a new prince to burden those who have submitted to him with his soldiery and countless other hardships.

So you have as enemies everyone you injured in seizing the principality, and you cannot keep as friends those who put you there, since you cannot satisfy them in the way they expected — and you cannot take strong measures against them, feeling bound to them. Though one may be very strong in armed forces, in entering a province one always needs the goodwill of the natives.

For these reasons Louis XII, King of France, quickly occupied Milan and as quickly lost it; to push him out the first time, Lodovico's own forces were enough. Those who had opened the gates to him, finding themselves disappointed in their hopes of future benefit, would not endure the ill-treatment of the new prince. It is true that, after acquiring rebellious provinces a second time, they are not so easily lost again; the prince, with little reluctance, uses the occasion of rebellion to punish offenders, clear out suspects, and strengthen himself in weak spots. So to make France lose Milan the first time it was enough for Duke Lodovico to raise insurrections on the borders; but to make him lose it a second time required that the whole world be brought against him, and that his armies be defeated and driven from Italy — which followed from the causes above.
Duke Lodovico was Lodovico Moro, son of Francesco Sforza, who married Beatrice d'Este. He ruled Milan from 1494 to 1500 and died in 1510.

Still, Milan was taken from France both the first and the second time. The general reasons for the first have been discussed; the second remains to be explained, along with what resources Louis had, and what anyone in his situation could have done to hold his acquisition more securely.

I say that dominions which, once acquired, are added to an ancient state are either of the same country and language as the acquirer's state or not. When they are, they are easier to hold, especially if they have not been used to self-government; to hold them securely it is enough to have destroyed the family of the prince who ruled them, because the two peoples, preserving their old conditions in other things and not differing in customs, will live quietly together — as seen in Brittany, Burgundy, Gascony, and Normandy, which have been bound to France for so long. Though there may be some difference in language, the customs are alike and the peoples will easily get on with each other. He who has annexed such places need only keep two things in mind: first, that the family of their former lord is extinguished; second, that neither their laws nor their taxes be altered, so that in a very short time they will become one body with the old principality.

But when states are acquired in a country differing in language, customs, or laws, there are difficulties, and good fortune and great energy are needed to hold them. One of the greatest and most real helps is for the acquirer to go and reside there. This makes his position more secure and lasting — as it has for the Turk in Greece, who, notwithstanding all the other measures he took, could not have held that state had he not settled there. When one is on the spot, disorders are seen as they arise and can quickly be remedied; when one is not at hand, they are heard of only when they are great, and then can no longer be remedied. Besides this, the country is not pillaged by your officials; subjects are satisfied by prompt access to the prince; so, wishing to be good, they have more reason to love him, and wishing to be otherwise, to fear him. Anyone who would attack the state from outside must use the utmost caution; as long as the prince resides there, it can only be wrested from him with the greatest difficulty.

The other and better course is to send colonies to one or two places that serve as keys to the state; otherwise one must keep a great number of cavalry and infantry there. A prince does not spend much on colonies: with little or no expense he can send them out and keep them there, and he offends only a minority of citizens — those from whom he takes lands and houses to give to the new inhabitants. Those he offends, remaining poor and scattered, are never able to injure him; the rest, being uninjured, are easily kept quiet, and at the same time anxious not to err for fear of being despoiled themselves. In conclusion, such colonies are inexpensive, more faithful, less injurious; and the injured, being poor and scattered, cannot hurt you. One must note this: men ought to be either well treated or crushed, because they can avenge themselves for light injuries but not for heavy ones; therefore any injury done to a man must be such that one need not fear his revenge.

But if one keeps armed men in place of colonies, one spends much more — consuming on the garrison all the state's income — so that the acquisition turns into a loss, and many more are exasperated, because the whole state is injured. As the garrison shifts up and down, all come to know hardship, and all become hostile — and they are enemies who, though beaten on their own ground, can still do harm. For every reason, then, such guards are as useless as a colony is useful.

The prince who holds a country differing in these respects should make himself the head and defender of his less powerful neighbors, and weaken the more powerful among them, taking care that no foreigner as powerful as himself gain a foothold there by any accident. A foreigner will always be brought in by the discontented, either through excess of ambition or through fear, as has been seen. The Romans were brought into Greece by the Aetolians, and in every other country where they gained a foothold they were brought in by the inhabitants. The usual course is this: as soon as a powerful foreigner enters a country, all the subject states are drawn to him, moved by their hatred of the ruling power. So for these subject states he need not take any trouble to gain them over; they all rally quickly to the state he has acquired there. He has only to take care that they do not get too much power and authority; with his own forces and their goodwill he can easily keep down the more powerful, so as to remain entirely master in the country. Anyone who does not properly manage this business will soon lose what he has acquired, and while he holds it will have endless difficulties and troubles.

The Romans, in the countries they annexed, closely observed these measures: they sent colonies, maintained friendly relations with minor powers without increasing their strength, kept down the greater, and did not allow any strong foreign powers to gain authority. Greece is example enough. The Achaeans and Aetolians were kept friendly; the kingdom of Macedonia was humbled; Antiochus was driven out. Yet the merits of the Achaeans and Aetolians never secured them permission to increase their power; nor did Philip's persuasions induce the Romans to be his friends without first humbling him; nor did Antiochus' influence make them agree to his retaining any lordship in the country. The Romans did what all prudent princes ought to do: regard not only present troubles but future ones too, and prepare for them with every energy. When foreseen, troubles are easy to remedy; but if you wait until they come upon you, the medicine is no longer in time, because the malady has become incurable. It is in affairs of state as physicians say of hectic fever: in its beginnings it is easy to cure but hard to detect; in the course of time, not having been detected or treated early, it becomes easy to detect but hard to cure. When evils are foreseen (which only a wise man can do), they can be quickly redressed; but when, through not having been foreseen, they have been allowed to grow to a point visible to everyone, there is no longer a remedy. So the Romans, foreseeing troubles, dealt with them at once and, even to avoid a war, would not let them come to a head; they knew war is not to be avoided, only deferred to another's advantage. They also wished to fight Philip and Antiochus in Greece so as not to have to fight them in Italy; they could have avoided both, but they did not wish to. Nor did they ever please themselves with what is forever on the lips of the supposed wise men of our time — "enjoy the benefits of the moment" — but rather the benefits of their own courage and prudence. For time drives everything before it, and can bring good as well as evil, evil as well as good.
See the note in the introduction on the word "intrattenere."

But let us turn to France and ask whether she has done any of the things mentioned. I will speak of Louis (not Charles), since his conduct is more instructive to observe, he having held Italy for the longest period; you will see he did the opposite of what ought to be done to retain a state composed of diverse elements.
Louis XII, King of France, "the Father of the People," born 1462, died 1515.
Charles VIII, King of France, born 1470, died 1498.

King Louis was brought into Italy by the ambition of the Venetians, who wished to obtain half of Lombardy through his intervention. I will not blame the course taken by the king: wishing to get a foothold in Italy and having no friends there — every door being shut to him because of Charles's conduct — he was forced to accept whatever friendships he could get. He would have succeeded quickly in his design had he not made some mistakes on other points. Having acquired Lombardy, the king regained at once the authority Charles had lost: Genoa yielded; the Florentines became his friends; the Marquess of Mantua, the Duke of Ferrara, the Bentivogli, my lady of Forlì, the lords of Faenza, Pesaro, Rimini, Camerino, Piombino, the Lucchese, the Pisans, the Sienese — everyone made advances to become his friend. Then the Venetians could see the rashness of their own course: to secure two towns in Lombardy, they had made the king master of two-thirds of Italy.

Consider how easily the king could have maintained his position in Italy had he observed the rules above and kept all his friends secure and protected. They were numerous but weak and timid — some afraid of the Church, some of the Venetians — and would always have been forced to stand with him; through them he could easily have made himself secure against those who remained powerful. But no sooner was he in Milan than he did the opposite, helping Pope Alexander to occupy the Romagna. It never occurred to him that by this action he was weakening himself, depriving himself of friends and of those who had thrown themselves into his lap, while he aggrandized the Church by adding much temporal power to the spiritual, thus giving it greater authority. Having committed this first error, he was obliged to follow it up: to put an end to Alexander's ambition and prevent him from becoming master of Tuscany, he was forced to come into Italy himself.

And as if it were not enough to have aggrandized the Church and deprived himself of friends, he, wishing to have the Kingdom of Naples, divided it with the King of Spain. Where he had been the prime arbiter in Italy, he took on an associate — giving the ambitious men of that country and the malcontents of his own a place to shelter. He could have left in the kingdom his own pensioner as king; instead he drove him out to put there one who was able to drive him, Louis, out in turn.

The wish to acquire is truly very natural and common, and men always do so when they can; for this they are praised, not blamed. But when they cannot and yet wish to do so by any means, there is folly and blame. So if France could have attacked Naples with her own forces, she ought to have done so; if not, she ought not to have divided it. If the partition with the Venetians in Lombardy was justified by the excuse that by it she got a foothold in Italy, this other partition deserved blame, since it had no such excuse of necessity.

So Louis made these five errors: he destroyed the minor powers; he increased the strength of one of the greater powers in Italy; he brought in a foreign power; he did not settle in the country; he did not send colonies. These errors, had he lived, might not have been enough to injure him had he not made a sixth by depriving the Venetians of their dominions. Had he not aggrandized the Church or brought Spain into Italy, it would have been reasonable and necessary to humble the Venetians; but having already taken those steps, he ought never to have consented to their ruin. Being powerful, they would always have kept others off designs on Lombardy, which the Venetians would never have consented to except to become masters themselves, and which the others would not have taken from France to give to the Venetians; and to set themselves against both, they would not have had the courage.

If anyone should say, "King Louis yielded the Romagna to Alexander and the kingdom to Spain to avoid war," I answer, for the reasons given, that a blunder ought never to be committed to avoid war — war is not to be avoided, only deferred to your disadvantage. And if someone should cite the pledge the king had given to the Pope to assist him in this enterprise in exchange for the dissolution of his marriage and the cardinal's cap for Rouen, to that I reply what I shall write later concerning the faith of princes and how it ought to be kept.
Louis XII divorced his wife Jeanne, daughter of Louis XI, and married in 1499 Anne of Brittany, widow of Charles VIII, in order to retain the Duchy of Brittany for the crown.
The Archbishop of Rouen was Georges d'Amboise, made cardinal by Alexander VI. Born 1460, died 1510.

Thus King Louis lost Lombardy by not following any of the conditions observed by those who have taken possession of countries and wished to retain them. There is no miracle in this, only what is reasonable and natural. I spoke of these matters at Nantes with Rouen, when Valentino (the usual name for Cesare Borgia, son of Pope Alexander) was occupying the Romagna. Cardinal Rouen remarked that the Italians did not understand war; I replied that the French did not understand statecraft, meaning that otherwise they would not have allowed the Church to grow so great. And in fact the greatness of the Church and of Spain in Italy has been caused by France, and their ruin may be attributed to them. From this a general rule can be drawn that rarely fails: he who makes another powerful ruins himself — for that predominance is brought about either by astuteness or by force, and both are distrusted by the one raised to power.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Why Darius's Kingdom Did Not Rebel Against Alexander's Successors
paragraphs: Considering the difficulties men have had in holding a newly acquired state, some might wonder how, seeing that Alexander the Great became master of Asia in a few years and died while it was scarcely settled (so that it would seem reasonable for the whole empire to have rebelled), his successors nevertheless maintained themselves, meeting no difficulty other than what arose among themselves from their own ambitions.

I answer that principalities of which we have record are governed in two different ways: either by a prince with a body of servants who assist him as ministers by his favor and permission, or by a prince with barons who hold their dignity by antiquity of blood and not by the grace of the prince. Such barons have their own states and subjects, who recognize them as lords and hold them in natural affection. States governed by a prince and his servants hold their prince in higher consideration, since in the whole country no one else is recognized as superior to him; if they yield obedience to another, they do so as to a minister or official, bearing him no particular affection.

The examples of these two governments in our time are the Turk and the King of France. The entire monarchy of the Turk is governed by one lord; the others are his servants. Dividing his kingdom into sanjaks, he sends various administrators there and shifts them as he chooses. But the King of France is placed in the midst of an ancient body of lords, acknowledged by their own subjects and loved by them; they have their own prerogatives, which the king cannot take away except at his peril. Anyone who considers both states will see great difficulty in seizing that of the Turk, but great ease in holding it once conquered. The difficulties of seizing the Turk's kingdom are that the usurper cannot be called in by the princes of the kingdom, nor can he hope to be assisted by the revolt of those around the lord. The ministers, being all slaves and bondmen, can only be corrupted with great difficulty, and one can expect little advantage from them when they have been corrupted, since they cannot carry the people with them. Anyone who attacks the Turk must bear in mind that he will find him united, and will have to rely more on his own strength than on the revolt of others. But once the Turk has been conquered and routed in the field so that he cannot replace his armies, there is nothing to fear but the family of this prince; and once that is exterminated, there remains no one to fear, since the others have no credit with the people. Just as the conqueror did not rely on them before his victory, he need not fear them after it.

The contrary happens in kingdoms governed like that of France: one can easily enter there by winning over some baron of the kingdom, since there are always malcontents and those who desire change. Such men can open the way into the state and make the victory easy; but if you wish to hold it afterwards, you meet infinite difficulties, both from those who helped you and from those you crushed. It is not enough to have exterminated the prince's family, because the remaining lords make themselves heads of fresh movements against you; and as you cannot either satisfy or exterminate them, you lose the state whenever time brings the opportunity.

Now if you consider the nature of Darius's government, you will find it similar to the Turk's kingdom. So Alexander had only to overthrow him in the field and then take the country from him; after that victory, with Darius killed, the state remained secure for Alexander, for the reasons above. Had his successors been united, they would have enjoyed it securely and at their ease; there were no tumults in the kingdom except those they themselves provoked.

But it is impossible to hold with such tranquility states constituted like that of France. Hence those frequent rebellions against the Romans in Spain, France, and Greece, owing to the many principalities in those states; as long as the memory of them endured, the Romans always held an insecure possession. But with the power and long continuance of the empire, that memory faded, and the Romans then became secure possessors. Even fighting among themselves afterwards, each was able to attach to himself his own part of the country, according to the authority he had assumed there; and with the former lord's family exterminated, none but the Romans were acknowledged.

Remembering these things, no one will marvel at the ease with which Alexander held the empire of Asia, or at the difficulties others have had in keeping an acquisition — such as Pyrrhus and many more. This is not owing to the little or great ability of the conqueror, but to the lack of uniformity in the subject state.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Governing Cities That Lived Under Their Own Laws
paragraphs: When states that have been acquired, as described, have been accustomed to live under their own laws and in freedom, there are three courses for those who wish to hold them. First, ruin them. Second, reside there in person. Third, let them live under their own laws, drawing a tribute and establishing an oligarchy that will keep them friendly to you. Such a government, being the prince's creature, knows it cannot stand without his friendship and interest, and does its utmost to support him. So he who would keep a city accustomed to freedom will hold it more easily by the means of its own citizens than in any other way.

Consider the Spartans and the Romans. The Spartans held Athens and Thebes, establishing an oligarchy in each; nevertheless they lost them. The Romans, in order to hold Capua, Carthage, and Numantia, dismantled them — and did not lose them. They wished to hold Greece as the Spartans had, making it free and permitting its laws, and did not succeed; so to hold it they were forced to dismantle many cities in the country. There is no safe way to retain such cities except by ruining them. He who becomes master of a city accustomed to freedom and does not destroy it may expect to be destroyed by it; in rebellion it has always the watchword of liberty and its ancient privileges as a rallying point, which neither time nor benefits will ever make it forget. Whatever you do or provide against, they never forget that name or their privileges, unless they are disunited or dispersed; at every opportunity they immediately rally to them — as Pisa did after the hundred years she had been held in bondage by the Florentines.

But when cities or countries are accustomed to live under a prince, and his family is exterminated, the people, being on the one hand accustomed to obey and on the other no longer having their old prince, cannot agree on one from among themselves, nor do they know how to govern themselves. They are very slow to take up arms, and a prince can gain them to himself and secure them much more easily. But in republics there is more vitality, greater hatred, and more desire for vengeance, which will never allow the memory of their former liberty to rest; so the safest way is to destroy them, or to reside there.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — New Principalities Acquired by One's Own Arms and Ability
paragraphs: Let no one be surprised if, in speaking of entirely new principalities (as I am about to), I adduce the highest examples of both prince and state. Men walk almost always in paths beaten by others, imitating their deeds; yet they are unable to keep entirely to the ways of others or attain to the power of those they imitate. A wise man ought always to follow the paths beaten by great men and imitate those who have been supreme, so that if his ability does not equal theirs, at least it will savor of it. Let him act like the skilled archers who, designing to hit a mark that appears too far away, and knowing the limits of their bow, take aim much higher than the mark — not to reach so great a height with the arrow, but to be able, with the aid of so high an aim, to hit the mark they wish.

I say, then, that in entirely new principalities with a new prince, more or less difficulty is found in keeping them according to the greater or lesser ability of the acquirer. Since becoming a prince from a private station presupposes either ability or fortune, it is clear that one or the other of these will mitigate many difficulties. Still, he who has relied least on fortune is the most strongly established. And it helps matters when the prince, having no other state, is compelled to reside there in person.

To come to those who by their own ability and not through fortune have risen to be princes, I say that Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus, and the like are the most excellent examples. Though one may not discuss Moses, he having been a mere executor of God's will, he ought to be admired, if only for the favor that made him worthy to speak with God. But in considering Cyrus and others who acquired or founded kingdoms, all will be found admirable; and if their particular deeds and conduct are considered, they will not be found inferior to Moses's, though he had so great a preceptor. Examining their actions and lives, one cannot see that they owed anything to fortune beyond opportunity, which brought them the material to mold into the form that seemed best. Without that opportunity their powers of mind would have been extinguished; without those powers, the opportunity would have come in vain.

It was necessary, then, that Moses find the people of Israel in Egypt enslaved and oppressed by the Egyptians, so that they would be disposed to follow him to be delivered from bondage. It was necessary that Romulus not remain in Alba, and that he be abandoned at birth, so that he should become King of Rome and founder of the fatherland. It was necessary that Cyrus find the Persians discontented with the government of the Medes, and the Medes soft and effeminate through long peace. Theseus could not have shown his ability had he not found the Athenians dispersed. These opportunities, then, made those men fortunate, and their high ability enabled them to recognize the opportunity by which their country was ennobled and made famous.

Those who, by valorous ways, become princes like these men acquire a principality with difficulty but keep it with ease. The difficulties of acquiring it arise partly from the new rules and methods they are forced to introduce to establish their government and its security. It should be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in success than to take the lead in introducing a new order of things. The innovator has as enemies all those who have done well under the old conditions, and lukewarm defenders in those who may do well under the new. This coolness arises partly from fear of opponents who have the laws on their side, and partly from the incredulity of men, who do not readily believe in new things until they have had long experience of them. So whenever those hostile find an opportunity to attack, they do it like partisans, while the others defend lukewarmly — and the prince is endangered along with them.

To discuss this matter thoroughly, we must ask whether these innovators can rely on themselves or must depend on others; whether, to carry through their enterprise, they must use prayers or can use force. In the first case they always succeed badly and never accomplish anything; but when they can rely on themselves and use force, they are rarely endangered. Hence all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. Besides the reasons mentioned, the nature of the people is variable; while it is easy to persuade them, it is difficult to fix them in that persuasion. So one must take such measures that, when they no longer believe, it is possible to make them believe by force.

If Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus had been unarmed, they could not have enforced their constitutions for long — as happened in our time to Fra Girolamo Savonarola, who was ruined with his new order of things as soon as the multitude believed in him no longer, and he had no means of keeping steadfast those who believed or of making the unbelievers believe. Such men, then, have great difficulties in consummating their enterprise; all their dangers are in the ascent, yet with ability they will overcome them. Once they are overcome, and those who envied their success are exterminated, they begin to be respected, and continue afterwards powerful, secure, honored, and happy.

To these great examples I wish to add a lesser one, which still bears some resemblance to them and can stand for all of its kind: Hiero of Syracuse. This man rose from a private station to be Prince of Syracuse; nor did he owe anything to fortune but opportunity. The Syracusans, being oppressed, chose him for their captain; afterwards he was rewarded by being made their prince. He was of such great ability, even as a private citizen, that one who writes of him says he wanted nothing but a kingdom to be a king. He abolished the old soldiery, organized the new, gave up old alliances, made new ones; and having his own soldiers and allies, on such foundations he could build any edifice. Having endured much trouble in acquiring, he had little trouble in keeping.
Hiero II, born about 307 BC, died 216 BC.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — New Principalities Acquired by the Arms of Others or by Good Fortune
paragraphs: Those who rise from private citizens to princes solely by good fortune have little trouble in rising, but much in keeping their position. They have no difficulties on the way up, since they fly; but many when they reach the summit. Such are those given a state either for money or by the favor of the giver, as happened to many in Greece, in the cities of Ionia and the Hellespont, where princes were made by Darius to hold the cities both for his security and his glory; also those emperors who, through the corruption of the soldiers, rose from citizens to empire. Such stand simply elevated on the goodwill and fortune of those who elevated them — two most inconstant and unstable things. Nor do they have the knowledge requisite for the position; unless they are men of great worth and ability, it is not reasonable to expect they should know how to command, having always lived as private citizens. Besides, they cannot hold power, since they have no forces they can keep friendly and faithful.

States that arise unexpectedly, like all other things in nature that are born and grow rapidly, cannot leave their foundations and relations fixed in such a way that the first storm will not overthrow them — unless, as said, those who unexpectedly become princes are of such ability that they know they must prepare at once to hold what fortune has thrown in their laps; the foundations others laid before becoming princes, they must lay afterwards.
"Le radici e corrispondenze" — their roots (foundations) and relations with other states; a common sense of "correspondence" in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

Concerning these two methods of rising to be a prince — by ability or by fortune — I wish to adduce two examples within our own memory: Francesco Sforza and Cesare Borgia. Francesco, by proper means and great ability, rose from a private person to be Duke of Milan, and what he had acquired with a thousand anxieties he kept with little trouble. Cesare Borgia, called Duke Valentino by the people, acquired his state during his father's ascendancy and lost it with his father's decline — though he had taken every measure and done all that a wise and able man ought to do to fix his roots firmly in the states that the arms and fortunes of others had bestowed on him.

Francesco Sforza, born 1401, died 1466. He married Bianca Maria Visconti, natural daughter of Filippo Visconti, Duke of Milan, on whose death he procured his own elevation to the duchy. Machiavelli was the accredited agent of the Florentine Republic to Cesare Borgia (1478–1507) during the transactions leading up to the assassinations of the Orsini and Vitelli at Sinigaglia. Along with his letters to his chiefs in Florence, he has left an account, written ten years before The Prince, of the duke's proceedings, in his "Descritione del modo tenuto dal duca Valentino nello ammazzare Vitellozzo Vitelli," etc., translated and appended to the present work.

As stated, he who has not first laid his foundations may, with great ability, lay them afterwards, but with trouble to the architect and danger to the building. If all the duke's steps are considered, it will be seen that he laid solid foundations for his future power. I do not consider it superfluous to discuss them, since I do not know what better precepts to give a new prince than the example of his actions; and if his arrangements were of no avail, that was not his fault but the extraordinary and extreme malignity of fortune.

Alexander VI, wishing to aggrandize the duke his son, had many immediate and prospective difficulties. First, he saw no way to make him master of any state not belonging to the Church; and if he was willing to rob the Church, he knew the Duke of Milan and the Venetians would not consent, Faenza and Rimini being already under Venetian protection. Besides, the arms of Italy, especially those that might have helped him, were in hands — the Orsini, the Colonnesi, and their following — that would fear the Pope's aggrandizement. It behooved him, then, to upset these arrangements and embroil the powers, so as to make himself securely master of part of their states. This was easy: he found the Venetians, moved by other reasons, inclined to bring the French back into Italy; he would not only not oppose this but render it easier by dissolving King Louis's former marriage. So the king came into Italy with Venetian assistance and Alexander's consent. He was no sooner in Milan than the Pope had soldiers from him for the Romagna enterprise, which yielded to him on the king's reputation. The duke, having acquired the Romagna and beaten the Colonnesi, wished to hold that and advance further, but was hindered by two things: his forces did not appear loyal to him, and the goodwill of France was uncertain. He feared the Orsini forces he was using would not stand by him, and that not only might they hinder further winnings but seize what he had won; and that the king might do the same. He had a warning about the Orsini when, after taking Faenza and attacking Bologna, he saw them go very unwillingly to that attack. As for the king, he learned his mind when, after taking the Duchy of Urbino, the duke attacked Tuscany and the king made him desist. So the duke decided to depend no more on the arms and luck of others.

His first step was to weaken the Orsini and Colonnesi parties in Rome, by winning to himself all their noble adherents — making them his gentlemen, giving them good pay, and, according to their rank, honoring them with office and command. In a few months all attachment to the factions was destroyed and turned entirely to the duke. He then awaited an opportunity to crush the Orsini, having scattered the Colonna house's adherents. The chance came soon, and he used it well. The Orsini, at length perceiving that the aggrandizement of the duke and the Church was their ruin, called a meeting at Magione in Perugia. From this sprang the rebellion at Urbino and the tumults in the Romagna, with endless dangers for the duke, all of which he overcame with French help. Having restored his authority, and not wishing to leave it at risk by trusting the French or other outside forces, he resorted to guile, and concealed his mind so well that, through the mediation of Signor Pagolo — whom the duke did not fail to secure with every attention, giving him money, apparel, and horses — the Orsini were reconciled. Their simplicity brought them into his power at Sinigaglia. Having exterminated the leaders and turned their partisans into his friends, the duke laid sufficiently good foundations for his power, holding all the Romagna and the Duchy of Urbino. The people, now beginning to appreciate their prosperity, he gained wholly to himself. Since this point is worthy of notice and fit to be imitated, I will not leave it out.
Sinigaglia, 31 December 1502.

When the duke occupied the Romagna, he found it under weak masters who rather plundered their subjects than ruled them, giving them more cause for disunion than for union. The country was full of robbery, quarrels, and every kind of violence. Wishing to restore peace and obedience to authority, he thought it necessary to give it a good governor. He promoted Messer Ramiro d'Orco, a swift and cruel man, to whom he gave full power. In a short time this man restored peace and unity with great success. Afterwards the duke considered it unwise to confer such excessive authority, fearing it would breed hatred; so he set up a court of judgment in the country under a most excellent president, in which all cities had their advocates. Knowing that the past severity had caused some hatred against himself, and to clear himself in the people's minds and win them entirely, he wished to show that if any cruelty had been practiced, it had originated not with him but in the minister's natural sternness. Under this pretext he seized Ramiro and one morning had him executed and left on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife beside him. The barbarity of this spectacle left the people at once satisfied and dismayed.
Ramiro d'Orco: Ramiro de Lorqua.

But to return where we began. The duke, now sufficiently powerful and partly secured from immediate dangers — having armed himself in his own way and largely crushed neighboring forces that could injure him if he wished to proceed with his conquest — had next to consider France. He knew that the king, belatedly aware of his mistake, would not support him. So he began to seek new alliances and to temporize with France in her expedition toward the Kingdom of Naples against the Spaniards besieging Gaeta. He intended to secure himself against the Spaniards, which he would have quickly accomplished had Alexander lived.

Such was his line of action as to present affairs. As for the future, he had to fear, first, that a new successor to the Church might not be friendly to him and might try to take back what Alexander had given him. So he decided to act in four ways. First, by exterminating the families of those lords whom he had despoiled, so as to take away that pretext from the Pope. Second, by winning over all the gentlemen of Rome, to curb the Pope with their help, as noted. Third, by bringing the college over more to himself. Fourth, by acquiring so much power before the Pope should die that he could by his own measures resist the first shock. At Alexander's death he had accomplished three of these four. He had killed as many dispossessed lords as he could lay hands on — few had escaped. He had won over the Roman gentlemen, and he had the most numerous party in the college. As for fresh acquisition, he intended to master Tuscany: he already possessed Perugia and Piombino, and Pisa was under his protection. Having no longer to study France (the French were already driven from Naples by the Spaniards, and both were compelled to buy his goodwill), he pounced on Pisa. Lucca and Siena then yielded at once, partly from hatred and partly from fear of the Florentines; the Florentines would have had no remedy had he continued to prosper as he was the year Alexander died. He had acquired so much power and reputation that he would have stood by himself, no longer depending on the luck and forces of others but solely on his own power and ability.

But Alexander died five years after he had first drawn the sword. He left the duke with only the state of the Romagna consolidated, the rest up in the air, between two most powerful hostile armies, and sick unto death. Yet in the duke there was such boldness and ability, and he knew so well how men are won or lost, and so firm were the foundations he had laid in so short a time, that if he had not had those armies on his back — or had he been in good health — he would have overcome all difficulties. His foundations were good: the Romagna waited for him more than a month; in Rome, though half alive, he remained secure; and while the Baglioni, the Vitelli, and the Orsini might come to Rome, they could not effect anything against him. If he could not make Pope whomever he wished, at least the one he did not wish would not have been elected. Had he been in sound health at Alexander's death, everything would have been different. On the day Julius II was elected, he told me he had thought of everything that might occur at his father's death and had provided a remedy for all — except that he had never anticipated that when the death came, he himself would be on the point of dying.
Alexander VI died of fever, 18 August 1503.
Julius II was Giuliano della Rovere, Cardinal of San Pietro ad Vincula, born 1443, died 1513.

Recalling all the duke's actions, I do not know how to blame him; rather, as I have said, I should hold him up as an example to all those who, by others' fortune or arms, are raised to government. Having a lofty spirit and far-reaching aims, he could not have regulated his conduct otherwise; only the shortness of Alexander's life and his own sickness frustrated his designs. Anyone who thinks it necessary, in a new principality, to secure himself, to win friends, to overcome either by force or fraud, to make himself beloved and feared by the people, to be followed and revered by the soldiers, to exterminate those with power or reason to hurt him, to change the old order for new, to be severe and gracious, magnanimous and liberal, to destroy a disloyal soldiery and create new, to maintain friendship with kings and princes in such a way that they must help him zealously and offend him cautiously — he cannot find a more vivid example than this man's actions.

He can be blamed only for the election of Julius II, in which he made a bad choice. Not being able to elect a Pope to his own liking, he could have hindered any other from being elected; and he ought never to have consented to any cardinal he had injured, or who had cause to fear him if made pontiff. For men injure either from fear or hatred. Those he had injured included San Pietro ad Vincula, Colonna, San Giorgio, and Ascanio. The rest, on becoming Pope, had to fear him, excepting Rouen and the Spaniards: the latter by their relationship and obligations, the former by his influence, since the Kingdom of France had relations with him. Above all, then, the duke ought to have had a Spaniard made Pope, and failing that, should have consented to Rouen and not San Pietro ad Vincula. He who believes that new benefits will cause great personages to forget old injuries is deceived. So the duke erred in his choice, and it was the cause of his ultimate ruin.
San Giorgio is Raffaello Riario. Ascanio is Ascanio Sforza.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — Those Who Have Obtained a Principality by Wickedness
paragraphs: Although a prince may rise from a private station in two further ways — neither entirely attributable to fortune or genius — I must not pass them over, though they could be more fully treated in a discussion of republics. These methods are: either rising to the principality by some wicked or nefarious means, or becoming prince of one's country by the favor of one's fellow citizens. Of the first, I will give two examples — one ancient, one modern — and without going further into the subject, I think these two will suffice for those who may be compelled to follow them.

Agathocles the Sicilian became King of Syracuse from not merely a private but a low and abject station. The son of a potter, he led an infamous life through all changes of fortune; yet he accompanied his infamies with such ability of mind and body that, devoting himself to the military profession, he rose through its ranks to be Praetor of Syracuse. Established in that position, and having deliberately resolved to make himself prince — and to seize by violence, without obligation to others, what had been granted him by consent — he came to an understanding with Hamilcar the Carthaginian, whose army was fighting in Sicily. One morning he assembled the people and senate of Syracuse, as if to discuss affairs of the republic; at a given signal the soldiers killed all the senators and the richest citizens. With them dead, he seized and held the princedom of the city without any civil disorder. Though twice routed by the Carthaginians and ultimately besieged, he was able to defend his city; and, leaving part of his men for defense, with the rest he attacked Africa and in a short time raised the siege of Syracuse. The Carthaginians, reduced to extreme necessity, were compelled to come to terms with Agathocles, leaving Sicily to him and contenting themselves with Africa.
Agathocles the Sicilian, born 361 BC, died 289 BC.

Whoever considers this man's actions and genius will see nothing, or little, that can be attributed to fortune. As shown, he attained preeminence not by anyone's favor but step by step in the military profession, gaining those steps with a thousand troubles and perils, and afterwards boldly holding them through many hazardous dangers. Yet it cannot be called talent to slay fellow citizens, betray friends, be without faith, mercy, or religion. Such methods may gain empire, but not glory. Still, if one considers Agathocles's courage in entering and extricating himself from dangers, together with his greatness of mind in enduring and overcoming hardships, one cannot see why he should be esteemed less than any notable captain. Nevertheless, his barbarous cruelty and inhumanity, with infinite wickedness, do not allow him to be celebrated among the most excellent men. What he achieved cannot be attributed to either fortune or genius.

In our times, during the rule of Alexander VI, Oliverotto da Fermo, having been left an orphan many years before, was brought up by his maternal uncle Giovanni Fogliani and sent in early youth to fight under Pagolo Vitelli, that, trained under his discipline, he might attain some high military position. After Pagolo died, he fought under his brother Vitellozzo, and in a short time, being endowed with wit and a vigorous body and mind, he became the first man in his profession. But finding it paltry to serve under others, he resolved, with the help of some citizens of Fermo to whom their country's slavery was dearer than its liberty, and with the Vitelleschi's aid, to seize Fermo. He wrote to Giovanni Fogliani that, having been away from home many years, he wished to visit him and the city and in some measure look upon his patrimony; and although he had labored to acquire only honor, yet, that the citizens might see he had not spent his time in vain, he wished to come honorably, accompanied by one hundred horsemen — his friends and retainers. He asked Giovanni to arrange that he be honorably received by the Fermians, which would be to his own honor as well as to Giovanni's, as his guardian.

Giovanni, then, did not fail in any attention due his nephew. He caused Oliverotto to be honorably received by the Fermians and lodged him in his own house. Having passed a few days and arranged what was necessary for his wicked design, Oliverotto gave a solemn banquet, to which he invited Giovanni Fogliani and the chiefs of Fermo. When the food and the usual entertainments were over, Oliverotto artfully began certain grave discourses about the greatness of Pope Alexander and his son Cesare and their enterprises. Giovanni and others replied; but he rose at once, saying such matters ought to be discussed in a more private place, and withdrew to a chamber, where Giovanni and the rest followed him. No sooner were they seated than soldiers issued from hidden places and slaughtered Giovanni and the others. After these murders, Oliverotto mounted his horse, rode up and down the town, and besieged the chief magistrate in his palace; in fear, the people were forced to obey him and form a government of which he made himself prince. He killed all malcontents who could injure him and strengthened himself with new civil and military ordinances, so that in the year he held the principality he was not only secure in Fermo but had become formidable to all his neighbors. His destruction would have been as difficult as Agathocles's had he not let himself be overreached by Cesare Borgia, who took him with the Orsini and Vitelli at Sinigaglia, as stated above. Thus, one year after committing this parricide, he was strangled together with Vitellozzo — the man he had made his leader in valor and wickedness.

Some may wonder how Agathocles and his like, after infinite treacheries and cruelties, could live long and secure in their country, defend themselves against external enemies, and never be conspired against by their own citizens — while many others, by means of cruelty, have not been able, even in peaceful times, to hold the state, still less in the doubtful times of war. I believe this follows from cruelty being badly or well used. Those can be called well used, if of evil it is possible to speak well, which are applied at one blow, are necessary to one's security, and are not persisted in afterwards unless they can be turned to the subjects' advantage. The badly employed are those which, though few at the outset, multiply with time rather than decrease. Those who practice the first system are able, with God's or man's aid, to mitigate their rule in some degree, as Agathocles did. It is impossible for those who follow the other to maintain themselves.
Mr. Burd suggests this word comes nearer Machiavelli's thought when he speaks of "crudeltà" than the more obvious "cruelties."

Note, then, that in seizing a state the usurper ought to examine closely all the injuries he must inflict and do them all at one stroke, so as not to have to repeat them daily. By not unsettling men, he will be able to reassure them and win them to himself by benefits. He who does otherwise, either from timidity or bad advice, is always compelled to keep the knife in his hand; he cannot rely on his subjects, nor can they attach themselves to him, owing to their continued and repeated wrongs. Injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less. Benefits ought to be given little by little, so their flavor may last longer.

Above all, a prince ought to live among his people in such a way that no unexpected circumstances, good or evil, can make him change. If the need for this comes in troubled times, you are too late for harsh measures; mild ones will not help you, for they will be considered forced from you, and no one will feel under any obligation to you for them.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — The Civil Principality
paragraphs: Turning to the other point — where a leading citizen becomes prince of his country not by wickedness or intolerable violence, but by his fellow citizens' favor — this may be called a civil principality. Genius or fortune is not absolutely necessary to attain it, but rather a happy shrewdness. Such a principality is obtained either by the favor of the people or by the favor of the nobles. In all cities these two distinct parties are found, and from this it arises that the people do not wish to be ruled or oppressed by the nobles, while the nobles wish to rule and oppress the people; from these opposite desires one of three results emerges in cities: principality, self-government, or anarchy.

A principality is created either by the people or by the nobles, according to which has the opportunity. The nobles, seeing they cannot withstand the people, begin to cry up the reputation of one of their own and make him a prince, so that under his shadow they can give vent to their ambitions. The people, finding they cannot resist the nobles, likewise cry up the reputation of one of their own and make him a prince, to be defended by his authority. He who obtains sovereignty with the aid of the nobles maintains himself with more difficulty than he who comes to it by the people's aid. The former finds many around him who consider themselves his equals, and so he can neither rule them nor manage them to his liking. But he who reaches sovereignty by popular favor stands alone, with none, or few, around him not prepared to obey him.

Besides, one cannot by fair dealing and without injury to others satisfy the nobles, but one can satisfy the people; their object is more righteous than that of the nobles — the latter wish to oppress, the former only not to be oppressed. A prince can never secure himself against a hostile people, since they are too many; but from the nobles he can secure himself, since they are few. The worst a prince can expect from a hostile people is to be abandoned; but from hostile nobles he has to fear not only abandonment but their rising against him. Being more far-seeing and astute in such affairs, they always come forward in time to save themselves and to gain favor with whomever they expect to prevail. The prince is compelled to live always with the same people, but can do without the same nobles, being able to make and unmake them daily, and to give or take away authority as it pleases him.

To make this clearer: the nobles ought to be looked at mainly in two ways. Either they shape their course in such a way as to bind themselves entirely to your fortune, or they do not. Those who bind themselves and are not rapacious ought to be honored and loved. Those who do not bind themselves may be dealt with in two ways: they may fail to do so from pusillanimity and natural want of courage, in which case you ought to use them — especially those who give good counsel; in prosperity you honor them, in adversity you need not fear them. But when, for their own ambitious ends, they shun binding themselves, it is a sign they are giving more thought to themselves than to you. A prince ought to guard against such and fear them as open enemies, since in adversity they always help ruin him.

Therefore, one who becomes a prince through the people's favor ought to keep them friendly, which he can easily do, since they ask only not to be oppressed. But one who, against the people, becomes a prince by the nobles' favor ought above all things to seek to win the people over, which he can do easily by taking them under his protection. When men receive good from one from whom they expected evil, they are bound more closely to their benefactor; the people thus become more devoted to him than if he had been raised to power by their own favors. A prince can win their affection in many ways — which, varying by circumstance, cannot be given as fixed rules — but I repeat: a prince must have the people friendly, otherwise he has no security in adversity.

Nabis, Prince of the Spartans, withstood an attack from all Greece and from a victorious Roman army, and against them defended his country and his government. To overcome this peril he had only to secure himself against a few; but this would not have been enough had the people been hostile. Let no one contradict this with the trite proverb "He who builds on the people builds on mud"; this is true when a private citizen makes such a foundation and persuades himself that the people will free him when oppressed by his enemies or the magistrates. He is very often deceived — as happened to the Gracchi in Rome and Messer Giorgio Scali in Florence. But given a prince established as described, who can command, is a man of courage, undismayed in adversity, does not fail in other qualifications, and by his resolution and energy keeps the whole people encouraged — he will never find himself deceived in them, and it will be shown that he has laid his foundations well.
Nabis, tyrant of Sparta, was conquered by the Romans under Flamininus in 195 BC; killed 192 BC.
Messer Giorgio Scali. This event is found in Machiavelli's Florentine History, Book III.

These principalities are liable to danger when passing from a civil to an absolute order of government, since such princes either rule personally or through magistrates. In the latter case their government is weaker and more insecure, resting entirely on the goodwill of those citizens raised to the magistracy, who — especially in troubled times — can destroy the government with great ease, either by intrigue or open defiance. The prince has no chance, amid tumults, to exercise absolute authority; citizens and subjects, accustomed to receive orders from magistrates, are not disposed to obey him in such confusions. And there will always be, in doubtful times, a scarcity of men he can trust. He cannot rely on what he observes in quiet times, when citizens have need of the state; then everyone agrees with him, everyone promises, and with death far off all wish to die for him. But in troubled times, when the state has need of its citizens, few are found. So much the more dangerous is this experiment, since it can only be tried once. A wise prince, therefore, ought to adopt such a course that his citizens will, in every circumstance, have need of the state and of him; then he will always find them faithful.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — How to Measure the Strength of Principalities
paragraphs: Another point must be considered in examining the character of these principalities: whether a prince has such power that, in case of need, he can support himself with his own resources, or whether he must always depend on the assistance of others. To be clear, I consider those able to support themselves by their own resources who can, through an abundance of men or money, raise a sufficient army to join battle against anyone who attacks them. I consider those always in need of others who cannot show themselves against the enemy in the field but are forced to defend themselves behind walls. The first case has been discussed, and we will speak of it again if it recurs. In the second, one can say nothing except to encourage such princes to provision and fortify their towns, and on no account to defend the open country. Whoever fortifies his town well, and has managed his subjects' concerns as stated, will never be attacked without great caution. Men are always averse to enterprises where difficulties are visible, and it will not be easy to attack one whose town is well fortified and who is not hated by his people.

The cities of Germany are absolutely free; they own but little country around them, and they obey the emperor when it suits them, fearing neither him nor any other nearby power. They are fortified in such a way that everyone thinks taking them by assault would be tedious and difficult: they have proper ditches and walls, enough artillery, and always keep public stores of food, drink, and firewood sufficient for a year. Beyond this, to keep the people quiet without loss to the state, they always have the means of providing work in those trades that are the city's life and strength, and on which the people are supported. They also hold military exercises in high repute and have many ordinances to uphold them.

So a prince who has a strong city, and has not made himself odious, will not be attacked — or if attacked, will be driven off with disgrace. The affairs of this world are so changeable that it is almost impossible to keep an army in the field for a whole year without interference. Someone might reply: if the people have property outside the city and see it burned, they will not remain patient; the long siege and self-interest will make them forget their prince. To this I answer that a powerful and courageous prince will overcome all such difficulties — at one moment giving his subjects hope that the evil will not last long, at another rousing fear of the enemy's cruelty, then adroitly guarding himself from any subjects who seem too bold.

Further, the enemy on arrival naturally burns and ruins the country while the people's spirits are still hot and ready for defense; so much the less, then, should the prince hesitate. After a time, when spirits have cooled, the damage is already done, the ills incurred, and there is no longer any remedy; the people are therefore so much the more ready to unite with their prince, he appearing to be under obligation to them now that their houses have been burned and possessions ruined in his defense. It is the nature of men to be bound by the benefits they confer as much as by those they receive. If everything is well considered, it will not be difficult for a wise prince to keep his citizens' minds steadfast from first to last, so long as he does not fail to support and defend them.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Ecclesiastical Principalities
paragraphs: It only remains to speak of ecclesiastical principalities. All their difficulties occur before taking possession; they are acquired either by ability or by good fortune, and can be held without either. They are sustained by the ancient ordinances of religion, which are so powerful and of such a character that principalities may be held no matter how their princes behave and live. These princes alone have states and do not defend them; they have subjects and do not rule them; and the states, though unguarded, are not taken from them, and the subjects, though not ruled, do not care — they have neither the desire nor the ability to alienate themselves. Such principalities alone are secure and happy. But being upheld by powers the human mind cannot reach, I shall speak no more of them: being exalted and maintained by God, it would be presumptuous and rash to discuss them.

Nevertheless, if someone should ask how the Church has attained such greatness in temporal power, seeing that from Alexander backwards the Italian potentates (not only those called so, but every baron and lord, however small) valued the temporal power very slightly — yet now a king of France trembles before it, and it has been able to drive him from Italy and to ruin the Venetians — though this is plain, it is not superfluous to recall it.

Before Charles, King of France, came into Italy, this country was under the dominion of the Pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the Florentines. These potentates had two principal anxieties: first, that no foreigner should enter Italy under arms; second, that none of themselves should seize more territory. Those about whom there was most anxiety were the Pope and the Venetians. To restrain the Venetians the union of all the others was needed, as in the defense of Ferrara; and to keep the Pope down they used the barons of Rome, who, divided into two factions — Orsini and Colonnesi — always had a pretext for disorder. Standing with arms in their hands under the Pope's eyes, they kept the papacy weak and powerless. Though a courageous pope such as Sixtus might sometimes arise, neither fortune nor wisdom could rid him of these nuisances. The short life of a pope is also a cause of weakness: in the ten years that is a pope's average life, he can with difficulty bring down one of the factions. If, for example, one pope nearly destroyed the Colonnesi, another would arise hostile to the Orsini and support the Colonnesi; and he would not have time to ruin the Orsini. This is why the temporal powers of the pope were little esteemed in Italy.
Charles VIII invaded Italy in 1494.

Alexander VI arose afterwards, who of all pontiffs that ever lived showed how a pope, with both money and arms, could prevail. Through the instrumentality of Duke Valentino, and by the French invasion, he brought about all those things I have discussed above in the duke's actions. Though his intention was to aggrandize the duke, not the Church, what he did nevertheless contributed to the Church's greatness; after his death and the duke's ruin, the Church became the heir of all his labors.

Pope Julius came next, and found the Church strong — possessing all the Romagna, the Roman barons reduced to impotence, their factions wiped out by Alexander's chastisements; he also found a way open to accumulate money in a manner not practiced before Alexander's time. Julius not only followed these things but improved on them, and intended to gain Bologna, ruin the Venetians, and drive the French from Italy. All these enterprises succeeded — so much the more to his credit, since he did everything to strengthen the Church and not any private person. He also kept the Orsini and Colonnesi factions within the bounds in which he found them; though they had some mind to cause disturbance, he held two things firm: the greatness of the Church, with which he terrified them; and not allowing them to have their own cardinals, who were the cause of disorders among them. Whenever these factions have their cardinals, they do not remain quiet for long; cardinals foster the factions in Rome and elsewhere, and the barons are compelled to support them, so disorders and tumults among the barons arise from the ambitions of prelates. For these reasons His Holiness Pope Leo found the papacy most powerful, and it is to be hoped that, if others made it great in arms, he will make it still greater and more venerated by his goodness and many other virtues.
Pope Leo X was Cardinal de' Medici.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Kinds of Soldiery and Mercenaries
paragraphs: Having discussed the characteristics of the principalities I first proposed to treat, considered to some degree the causes of their being good or bad, and shown the methods by which many have sought to acquire and hold them, it remains for me to discuss generally the means of offense and defense belonging to each.

We have seen how necessary it is for a prince to lay his foundations well; otherwise he must go to ruin. The chief foundations of all states, new as well as old or composite, are good laws and good arms. Since there cannot be good laws where the state is not well armed, it follows that where there are good arms there are good laws. I shall leave laws aside and speak of arms.

The arms with which a prince defends his state are either his own, or mercenaries, auxiliaries, or mixed. Mercenaries and auxiliaries are useless and dangerous; one who holds his state based on such arms will stand neither firm nor safe. They are disunited, ambitious, and undisciplined, unfaithful — valiant among friends, cowardly among enemies — with neither fear of God nor fidelity to men. Destruction is deferred only as long as the attack is; in peace you are robbed by them, in war by the enemy. They have no attraction or reason to stay in the field except a trifle of pay, which is not enough to make them willing to die for you. They are ready enough to be your soldiers while you do not make war; but if war comes, they take themselves off or run from the foe. This I could easily prove: the ruin of Italy has been caused by nothing other than resting all her hopes, for many years, on mercenaries. Though they formerly made some display and seemed valiant among themselves, when the foreigners came they showed what they were. Thus Charles, King of France, was allowed to seize Italy with chalk in hand; and he who told us our sins were the cause spoke the truth — but not the sins he imagined, rather those I have described. As they were the sins of princes, the princes have also suffered the penalty.

"With chalk in hand" ("col gesso") is one of Alexander VI's bons mots, referring to the ease with which Charles VIII seized Italy — implying he had only to send his quartermasters to chalk up billets for his soldiers. Lord Bacon's History of Henry VII puts it this way: "King Charles had conquered the realm of Naples, and lost it again, in a kind of felicity of a dream. He passed the whole length of Italy without resistance; as Pope Alexander used to say, the Frenchmen came into Italy with chalk in their hands to mark up their lodgings, rather than with swords to fight."

I wish to show further the infelicity of these arms. The mercenary captains are either capable men or they are not. If capable, you cannot trust them, since they always aspire to their own greatness, either by oppressing you — their master — or others contrary to your intentions. If the captain is unskilled, you are ruined in the usual way.

If it be urged that whoever is armed will act the same way, mercenary or not, I reply that when a prince or republic must resort to arms, the prince ought to go in person and perform the duty of captain; the republic must send its citizens, and when one sent does not turn out well, it ought to recall him; when one is worthy, to hold him by the laws so he does not overstep his command. Experience has shown that princes and republics acting on their own make the greatest progress, while mercenaries do nothing but damage. It is more difficult to bring a republic armed with its own arms under the sway of one of its citizens than to bring one armed with foreign arms. Rome and Sparta stood for many ages armed and free. The Swiss are completely armed and entirely free.

Among ancient mercenaries, consider the Carthaginians, oppressed by their mercenary soldiers after the first war with Rome, though the Carthaginians had their own citizens for captains. After Epaminondas's death, Philip of Macedon was made captain of their soldiers by the Thebans, and after victory he took away their liberty.

After Duke Filippo died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza against the Venetians; having overcome the enemy at Caravaggio, he allied with them to crush the Milanese, his masters. His father, Sforza, having been engaged by Queen Johanna of Naples, left her unprotected, so she was forced to throw herself into the arms of the King of Aragon to save her kingdom. If the Venetians and Florentines formerly extended their dominions by these arms without their captains making themselves princes, I reply that the Florentines were favored by chance: of the able captains they might have feared, some did not conquer, some were opposed, others turned their ambitions elsewhere. One who did not conquer was Giovanni Acuto, and since he did not conquer his fidelity cannot be proved; but everyone will admit that, had he conquered, the Florentines would have stood at his discretion. Sforza always had the Bracceschi against him, so they watched each other. Francesco turned his ambition to Lombardy; Braccio against the Church and the Kingdom of Naples. But let us come to what happened a short while ago. The Florentines appointed as their captain Pagolo Vitelli, a most prudent man who rose from a private position to the greatest renown. Had this man taken Pisa, no one can deny it would have been proper for the Florentines to keep in with him; if he became the soldier of their enemies, they had no way to resist; if they held him, they had to obey him. The Venetians, if their actions are considered, will be seen to have acted safely and gloriously as long as they sent their own men to war — when with armed gentlemen and plebeians they behaved valiantly. This was before they turned to enterprises on land; once they began to fight on land, they forsook this virtue and followed the custom of Italy. In the beginning of their land expansion, not having much territory and having a great reputation, they had little to fear from their captains; but when they expanded, as under Carmignuola, they tasted this mistake. Finding him most valiant (they beat the Duke of Milan under him) but also knowing how lukewarm he was in war, they feared they would no longer conquer under him; and for this reason they were unwilling and unable to let him go; so, not to lose what they had acquired, they were compelled, for their own security, to murder him. Afterwards their captains were Bartolomeo da Bergamo, Roberto da San Severino, the Count of Pitigliano, and the like — under whom they had to dread loss, not gain, as happened at Vailà, where in one battle they lost what in eight hundred years they had acquired with so much trouble. From such arms, conquests come slowly, long delayed, and inconsiderable, but losses are sudden and portentous.
Battle of Caravaggio, 15 September 1448.
Johanna II of Naples, widow of Ladislao, King of Naples.

Giovanni Acuto: an English knight whose name was Sir John Hawkwood. He fought in the English wars in France and was knighted by Edward III; afterwards he collected a body of troops and went to Italy. These became the famous "White Company." He took part in many wars and died in Florence in 1394. Born about 1320 at Sible Hedingham, a village in Essex. He married Donnina, a daughter of Bernabò Visconti.
Carmignuola: Francesco Bussone, born at Carmagnola about 1390, executed at Venice, 5 May 1432.

Bartolomeo Colleoni of Bergamo, died 1457. Roberto of San Severino, died fighting for Venice against Sigismund, Duke of Austria, in 1487 — "Primo capitano in Italia" (Machiavelli). Count of Pitigliano: Niccolò Orsini, born 1442, died 1510.
Battle of Vailà, 1509.

Since with these examples I have reached Italy, which has been ruled for many years by mercenaries, I wish to discuss them more seriously, so that, having seen their rise and progress, one may be better prepared to counteract them. You must understand that the empire has recently come to be repudiated in Italy, that the Pope has acquired more temporal power, and that Italy has been divided into more states. Many of the great cities took up arms against their nobles, who, formerly favored by the emperor, were oppressing them, while the Church favored them to gain authority in temporal power; in many other cities the citizens became princes. From this Italy fell partly into the hands of the Church and of republics; and since the Church consists of priests and the republic of citizens unaccustomed to arms, both began to hire foreigners.

The first to give renown to this soldiery was Alberigo da Conio, the Romagnol. From this man's school sprang, among others, Braccio and Sforza, who in their day were the arbiters of Italy. After them came all the other captains who have until now directed Italy's arms; and the end of all their valor has been that Italy has been overrun by Charles, robbed by Louis, ravaged by Ferdinand, and insulted by the Swiss. Their guiding principle has been, first, to lower the credit of infantry so as to raise their own. Living on their pay and without territory, they were unable to support many soldiers, and a few infantry gave them no authority; so they took to cavalry, with a moderate force of which they were maintained and honored. Things were brought to such a pass that, in an army of twenty thousand soldiers, two thousand foot soldiers could not be found. They had also used every art to lessen fatigue and danger to themselves and their soldiers, not killing in the fray but taking prisoners and releasing them without ransom. They did not attack towns at night, nor did the garrisons attack encampments at night; they did not surround the camp with stockade or ditch; they did not campaign in winter. All these were permitted by their military rules, devised to avoid fatigue and danger — and they have brought Italy to slavery and contempt.
Alberigo da Conio: Alberico da Barbiano, Count of Cunio in Romagna. He was the leader of the famous "Company of St. George," composed entirely of Italian soldiers. Died 1409.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Auxiliaries, Mixed Soldiery, and One's Own
paragraphs: Auxiliaries — the other useless arm — are employed when a prince is called in with his forces to aid and defend, as Pope Julius did recently. Having had poor proof of his mercenaries in the Ferrara enterprise, he turned to auxiliaries and contracted with Ferdinand, King of Spain, for assistance with men and arms. Such arms may be useful and good in themselves, but for the one who calls them in they are always disadvantageous: losing, one is undone; winning, one is their captive.
