Ferdinand V (F. II of Aragon and Sicily, F. III of Naples), surnamed "The Catholic," born 1452, died 1516.

Though ancient histories are full of examples, I do not wish to leave this recent one of Pope Julius II, whose peril cannot fail to be perceived. Wishing to get Ferrara, he threw himself entirely into the hands of the foreigner. But his good fortune brought about a third event, so that he did not reap the fruit of his rash choice: his auxiliaries were routed at Ravenna, and the Swiss rose and drove out the conquerors (against all expectation, his and others'); so he became prisoner neither of his enemies (who had fled) nor of his auxiliaries (having conquered by arms other than theirs).
The Florentines, entirely without arms, sent ten thousand Frenchmen to take Pisa — thereby running more danger than at any other time of their troubles.

The Emperor of Constantinople, to oppose his neighbors, sent ten thousand Turks into Greece; with the war finished, they refused to leave. This was the beginning of Greece's servitude to the infidels.
Joannes Cantacuzenus, born 1300, died 1383.

Let him, then, who has no desire to conquer make use of these arms; for they are far more hazardous than mercenaries. With auxiliaries, ruin is ready-made — they are all united, all yielding obedience to others. With mercenaries, when they have conquered, more time and better opportunities are needed to injure you: they are not all of one community, they are hired and paid by you, and a third party you have made their head cannot all at once assume enough authority to injure you. In conclusion: with mercenaries, cowardice is most dangerous; with auxiliaries, valor. The wise prince has therefore always avoided these arms and turned to his own; he has been willing rather to lose with his own than to conquer with the others, not deeming a real victory that which is won by others' arms.

I shall never hesitate to cite Cesare Borgia and his actions. This duke entered the Romagna with auxiliaries, bringing only French soldiers, and with them captured Imola and Forlì. Afterwards, such forces not appearing reliable, he turned to mercenaries as less dangerous, and enlisted the Orsini and Vitelli; but finding them, in handling, doubtful, unfaithful, and dangerous, he destroyed them and turned to his own men. The difference between these forces can easily be seen in the difference in the duke's reputation — when he had the French, when he had the Orsini and Vitelli, and when he relied on his own soldiers, on whose fidelity he could always count, and found it ever increasing. He was never more highly esteemed than when everyone saw he was complete master of his own forces.

I had not meant to go beyond Italian and recent examples, but I cannot leave out Hiero of Syracuse, one of those named above. Having been made head of the army by the Syracusans, he soon saw that a mercenary soldiery, constituted like our Italian condottieri, was useless; finding he could neither keep them nor let them go, he had them all cut to pieces, and afterwards made war with his own forces, not aliens.

I also wish to recall an example from the Old Testament. David offered himself to Saul to fight with Goliath, the Philistine champion; to give him courage, Saul armed him with his own weapons. David cast them off as soon as he had them on his back, saying he could make no use of them and wished to meet the enemy with his sling and his knife. In short: others' arms either fall from your back, weigh you down, or bind you fast.

Charles VII, father of King Louis XI, having by good fortune and valor liberated France from the English, recognized the necessity of being armed with his own forces; he established in his kingdom ordinances for men-at-arms and infantry. Afterwards his son, King Louis, abolished the infantry and began to enlist the Swiss — a mistake, followed by others, which is now seen as a source of peril to that kingdom. By raising the reputation of the Swiss, he has entirely diminished the value of his own arms, destroying the infantry altogether; and his men-at-arms he has subordinated to others, so accustomed to fighting alongside Swiss that they no longer seem able to conquer without them. Hence the French cannot stand against the Swiss, and without the Swiss they do not come off well against others. The French armies have thus become mixed — partly mercenary, partly national. These two together are much better than mercenaries alone or auxiliaries alone, but much inferior to one's own forces. This example proves it: the kingdom of France would be unconquerable if Charles's ordinance had been extended or maintained.
Charles VII of France, surnamed "The Victorious," born 1403, died 1461.
Louis XI, son of the above, born 1423, died 1483.

But the scanty wisdom of man, entering into an affair that looks well at first, cannot discern the poison hidden in it, as I said above of hectic fevers. If he who rules a principality cannot recognize evils until they are upon him, he is not truly wise; this insight is given to few. If the first disaster to the Roman Empire is examined, it will be found to have begun only with the enlistment of the Goths; from that time the vigor of the Roman Empire began to decline, and all the valor that had raised it passed away to others.

"Many speakers to the House the other night in the debate on the reduction of armaments seemed to show a most lamentable ignorance of the conditions under which the British Empire maintains its existence. When Mr. Balfour replied to the allegations that the Roman Empire sank under the weight of its military obligations, he said that this was 'wholly unhistorical.' He might well have added that the Roman power was at its zenith when every citizen acknowledged his liability to fight for the state, but began to decline as soon as this obligation was no longer recognized." — Pall Mall Gazette, 15 May 1906.

I conclude, then, that no principality is secure without its own forces; on the contrary, it is entirely dependent on good fortune, lacking the valor that would defend it in adversity. It has always been the opinion of wise men that nothing is so uncertain or unstable as fame or power not founded on its own strength. One's own forces are those composed of subjects, citizens, or dependents; all others are mercenaries or auxiliaries. The way to prepare one's own forces will easily be found by reflecting on the rules I have suggested, and by considering how Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, and many republics and princes have armed and organized themselves — to which examples I entirely commit myself.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — A Prince's Subject of War
paragraphs: A prince ought to have no other aim or thought, and select nothing else for his study, than war and its rules and discipline. This is the sole art that belongs to him who rules, and it is of such force that it not only upholds those born princes, but often enables men to rise from a private station to that rank. Conversely, when princes have thought more of ease than of arms, they have lost their states. The first cause of losing your state is to neglect this art; what enables you to acquire one is mastery of it. Francesco Sforza, through being martial, rose from a private person to Duke of Milan; his sons, by avoiding the hardships and troubles of arms, descended from dukes to private persons. Among other evils, being unarmed makes you despised — one of those ignominies a prince ought to guard against, as will be shown. There is nothing proportionate between the armed and the unarmed; it is not reasonable that the armed should willingly obey the unarmed, or that the unarmed should be secure among armed servants. With disdain in the one and suspicion in the other, they cannot work well together. A prince who does not understand the art of war, over and above the other misfortunes already mentioned, cannot be respected by his soldiers, nor rely on them. He ought never, then, to take his mind off this subject of war, and in peace should devote himself to it even more than in war. This he can do in two ways: by action and by study.

As for action, he ought above all to keep his men well organized and drilled, and to follow the chase incessantly. By hunting he accustoms his body to hardship and learns the nature of terrain — how mountains rise, how valleys open out, how plains lie, the nature of rivers and marshes — and in all this he should take great care. This knowledge is useful in two ways. First, he learns to know his own country and is better able to defend it. Second, with knowledge of one locality, he understands others more easily; the hills, valleys, plains, rivers, and marshes of, say, Tuscany have a certain resemblance to those of other countries, so that knowledge of one country's terrain leads easily to knowledge of others'. The prince who lacks this skill lacks what a captain should possess; it teaches him to surprise his enemy, select quarters, lead armies, arrange the battle, and besiege towns to advantage.

Philopoemen, Prince of the Achaeans, is praised among other things because in peacetime he had nothing in mind but the rules of war. When he was in the country with friends, he often stopped and reasoned with them: "If the enemy were on that hill, and we with our army here, who would have the advantage? How should we best advance to meet him, keeping ranks? If we wished to retreat, how should we do it?" As they went he would set forth every chance that could befall an army; he would listen to their opinions and state his own, supporting it with reasons. By these continual discussions there could never arise, in war, any unexpected circumstance he could not deal with.
Philopoemen, "the last of the Greeks," born 252 BC, died 183 BC.

To exercise the intellect, the prince should read histories and study the actions of illustrious men — how they bore themselves in war, the causes of their victories and defeats — so as to avoid the latter and imitate the former. Above all, he should do as an illustrious man did who took for a model one who had been praised and famous before him, keeping his achievements and deeds always in mind, as Alexander the Great imitated Achilles, Caesar imitated Alexander, and Scipio imitated Cyrus. Anyone who reads the life of Cyrus, written by Xenophon, will recognize in the life of Scipio how much that imitation contributed to his glory, and how in chastity, affability, humanity, and liberality Scipio conformed to what Xenophon wrote of Cyrus. A wise prince ought to observe such rules, and never in peaceful times stand idle, but industriously increase his resources, so that they may be available in adversity — so that if fortune turns, it finds him prepared to resist her blows.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Things for Which Princes Are Praised or Blamed
paragraphs: It remains to see what ought to be the rules of conduct for a prince toward his subjects and friends. Since many have written on this, I expect I shall be considered presumptuous in mentioning it again, especially as my discussion will depart from others' methods. But my intention is to write something useful to him who understands it; so it seems more fitting to follow the real truth of the matter than its imagination. Many have pictured republics and principalities that in fact have never been known or seen; for how one lives is so far from how one ought to live that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done will sooner bring about his ruin than his preservation. A man who wishes to act entirely up to his professions of virtue soon meets with what destroys him among so much that is evil.

It is therefore necessary for a prince wishing to hold his own to know how to do wrong, and to make use of it or not according to necessity. Setting aside imaginary things about princes, then, and discussing what is real: I say that all men, when spoken of — and chiefly princes, being more highly placed — are remarkable for some qualities that bring them blame or praise. One is reputed liberal, another miserly (using a Tuscan term, since an avaricious person in our language is one who desires to possess by robbery, while we call miserly one who deprives himself too much of the use of his own); one generous, one rapacious; one cruel, one compassionate; one faithless, another faithful; one effeminate and cowardly, another bold and brave; one affable, another haughty; one lascivious, another chaste; one sincere, another cunning; one hard, another easy; one grave, another frivolous; one religious, another unbelieving, and so on. Everyone will admit that it would be most praiseworthy for a prince to exhibit all the qualities considered good; but since they cannot all be possessed or observed — human conditions not permitting it — he must be prudent enough to know how to avoid the reproach of those vices that would lose him his state, and to keep himself, if possible, from those that would not lose it for him. But where that is not possible, he may abandon himself to them with less hesitation. And he need not worry about incurring a reproach for those vices without which the state can hardly be saved: if everything is carefully considered, something that looks like virtue, if followed, would be his ruin; while something else that looks like vice, if followed, brings him security and prosperity.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — Liberality and Meanness
paragraphs: Beginning, then, with the first of the characteristics above: it would be well to be reputed liberal. Nevertheless, liberality exercised in a way that does not bring you the reputation for it injures you. If you exercise it honestly and as it should be exercised, it may not become known, and you will not avoid the reproach of the opposite. Anyone wishing to keep the reputation of liberal among men is obliged to avoid no display of magnificence; a prince so inclined will consume all his property in such acts, and in the end, to keep the name of liberal, will be compelled to burden his people unduly, tax them, and do everything he can to get money. This will soon make him odious to his subjects, and in becoming poor he will be little valued by anyone. So, with his liberality, having offended many and rewarded few, he is affected by the very first trouble and imperiled by whatever danger comes first. Recognizing this, and wishing to draw back, he at once incurs the reproach of being miserly.

A prince, then, not being able to exercise liberality in a way that is recognized except at his cost, would be wise not to fear the reputation of being miserly. In time he will come to be more esteemed than if liberal: with his economy his revenues suffice, he can defend himself against all attacks, and can undertake enterprises without burdening his people. Thus he exercises liberality toward all from whom he does not take — numberless — and meanness only toward those to whom he does not give, who are few.

We have seen great things done in our time only by those considered mean; the rest have failed. Pope Julius II was helped to the papacy by a reputation for liberality, yet did not strive to keep it up afterwards, when he made war on the King of France; he made many wars without imposing any extraordinary tax on his subjects, supplying his extra expenses out of his long thriftiness. The present King of Spain would not have undertaken or conquered so many enterprises had he been reputed liberal. A prince, provided he need not rob his subjects, can defend himself, does not become poor and abject, and is not forced to become rapacious, ought to hold of little account a reputation for meanness — it is one of those vices that will enable him to govern.

If someone should say: Caesar obtained empire by liberality, and many others reached the highest positions by being, and being considered, liberal — I answer: either you are already a prince, or you are on the way to becoming one. In the first case, such liberality is dangerous; in the second, it is very necessary to be considered liberal. Caesar was one who wished to become preeminent in Rome; but if he had survived after becoming so and had not moderated his expenses, he would have destroyed his government. And if someone should reply: many princes have done great things with armies, and been considered very liberal — I answer: a prince spends either his own, his subjects', or that of others. In the first case he ought to be sparing; in the second he ought not to neglect any opportunity for liberality. A prince who goes forth with his army, supporting it by pillage, sack, and extortion, handling what belongs to others, must be liberal; otherwise he would not be followed by his soldiers. Of what is neither yours nor your subjects' you can be a ready giver, as Cyrus, Caesar, and Alexander were; squandering others' property does not take away your reputation but adds to it. It is only squandering your own that injures you.

Nothing wastes itself so rapidly as liberality; while you exercise it, you lose the power to do so, and become either poor and despised or, to avoid poverty, rapacious and hated. A prince should guard himself above all from being despised and hated; liberality leads to both. So it is wiser to have a reputation for meanness, which brings reproach without hatred, than to be compelled, through seeking a reputation for liberality, to incur a name for rapacity, which brings reproach with hatred.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — Cruelty and Clemency: Whether It Is Better to Be Loved Than Feared
paragraphs: Coming now to the other qualities mentioned above: every prince ought to desire to be considered clement and not cruel. Nevertheless he ought to take care not to misuse this clemency. Cesare Borgia was considered cruel; yet his cruelty reconciled the Romagna, unified it, and restored it to peace and loyalty. Rightly considered, he will be seen to have been much more merciful than the Florentine people, who, to avoid a reputation for cruelty, permitted Pistoia to be destroyed. A prince, then, so long as he keeps his subjects united and loyal, ought not to mind the reproach of cruelty; with a few examples he will be more merciful than those who, through too much mercy, allow disorders to arise that lead to murders or robberies. The latter injure the whole people; executions ordered by a prince offend only individuals.
During the rioting between the Cancellieri and Panciatichi factions in 1502–1503.

Of all princes, the new prince cannot avoid the imputation of cruelty, because new states are full of dangers. Hence Virgil, through the mouth of Dido, excuses the inhumanity of her reign by its newness:
"Res dura, et regni novitas me talia cogunt / Moliri, et late fines custode tueri."

Nevertheless a prince ought to be slow to believe and to act, nor should he himself show fear; he should proceed in a temperate manner with prudence and humanity, so that too much confidence does not make him incautious, nor too much distrust make him intolerable.
"…against my will, my fate / A throne unsettled, and an infant state, / Bid me defend my realms with all my powers, / And guard with these severities my shores."
Christopher Pitt.

A question arises here: is it better to be loved than feared, or feared than loved? One would wish to be both; but since it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, if one must be dispensed with. Of men in general this can be asserted: they are ungrateful, fickle, false, cowardly, covetous. As long as you succeed they are yours entirely; they will offer you their blood, property, life, and children, as said above, when the need is far distant; but when it approaches, they turn against you. A prince who relies entirely on their promises and has neglected other precautions is ruined. Friendships obtained by payments, and not by greatness or nobility of mind, may indeed be earned but not secured, and in time of need cannot be relied upon. Men have less scruple in offending one who is loved than one who is feared: love is preserved by a link of obligation which, owing to the baseness of men, is broken at every opportunity for their advantage; but fear preserves you by a dread of punishment that never fails.

Still, a prince ought to inspire fear in such a way that, if he does not win love, he avoids hatred. He can endure being feared very well as long as he is not hated — which he will avoid so long as he abstains from the property of his citizens and subjects and from their women. When it becomes necessary to proceed against someone's life, he must do it on proper justification and for manifest cause; but above all he must keep his hands off the property of others. Men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony. Pretexts for taking property are never lacking; he who has once begun to live by robbery will always find pretexts for seizing what belongs to others. Reasons for taking life, by contrast, are harder to find and sooner lapse. When a prince is with his army, and has under his control a multitude of soldiers, it is quite necessary for him to disregard the reputation of cruelty; without it he would never hold his army united or disposed to its duties.

Among Hannibal's wonderful deeds this is numbered: having led an enormous army composed of many races of men to fight in foreign lands, no dissensions arose among them or against their commander, in bad or in good fortune. This came from nothing else than his inhuman cruelty, which, with his boundless valor, made him revered and terrible to his soldiers; without that cruelty, his other virtues were not sufficient to produce this effect. Shortsighted writers admire his deeds from one point of view and from another condemn the principal cause of them. That his other virtues would not have been enough is shown by the case of Scipio, that most excellent man, not only of his own times but within human memory, against whom, nevertheless, his army in Spain rebelled. This came from nothing but his too great forbearance, which gave his soldiers more license than is consistent with military discipline. For this he was upbraided in the Senate by Fabius Maximus, and called the corrupter of Roman soldiery. The Locrians were laid waste by a legate of Scipio, yet they were not avenged by him, nor was the insolence of the legate punished — entirely owing to his easy nature. So much so that someone in the Senate, wishing to excuse him, said there were many men who knew much better how not to err themselves than how to correct the errors of others. This disposition, if he had remained in command, would in time have destroyed Scipio's fame and glory; but as he was under the control of the Senate, this injurious characteristic not only concealed itself but contributed to his glory.

Returning to the question of being feared or loved, I conclude: since men love according to their own will and fear according to the prince's, a wise prince should establish himself on what is in his own control, not what is in the control of others. He must endeavor only to avoid hatred, as noted.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — How Princes Should Keep Faith
paragraphs: "The present chapter has given greater offense than any other portion of Machiavelli's writings." — Burd, Il Principe, p. 297.

Everyone admits how praiseworthy it is in a prince to keep faith, and to live with integrity rather than craft. Nevertheless, experience has been that the princes who have done great things have held good faith of little account, and have known how to outwit men by craft; in the end they have overcome those who relied on their word. You must know that there are two ways of contending: by law, or by force. The first is proper to men, the second to beasts; but since the first is often not sufficient, one must have recourse to the second. It is necessary, then, for a prince to know how to make use of both the beast and the man. This was taught figuratively to princes by ancient writers, who describe how Achilles and many other princes of old were given to the centaur Chiron to nurse, who brought them up in his discipline. The meaning is simply that, as they had for a teacher one who was half beast and half man, so a prince must know how to make use of both natures, and one without the other is not durable. A prince compelled to adopt the beast ought to choose the fox and the lion: the lion cannot defend himself against snares, the fox cannot defend himself against wolves. One must be a fox to discover snares and a lion to terrify wolves. Those who rely simply on the lion do not understand what they are about. A wise lord cannot, nor ought he to, keep faith when such observance may be turned against him and when the reasons that caused him to pledge it no longer exist. If men were entirely good this precept would not hold; but because they are bad and will not keep faith with you, you are not bound to observe it with them. Nor will a prince ever lack legitimate reasons to excuse such non-observance. Endless modern examples could be given: how many treaties and engagements have been made void and of no effect through the faithlessness of princes; and he who has known best how to employ the fox has succeeded best.

"Contesting" means "striving for mastery." Mr. Burd points out that this passage is imitated directly from Cicero's De Officiis: "Nam cum sint duo genera decertandi, unum per disceptationem, alterum per vim; cumque illud proprium sit hominis, hoc beluarum; confugiendum est ad posterius, si uti non licet superiore."

It is necessary to know how to disguise this trait well, and to be a great pretender and dissembler. Men are so simple and so subject to present necessities that he who seeks to deceive will always find someone willing to be deceived. One recent example I cannot pass over. Alexander VI did nothing but deceive men; he never thought of doing otherwise, and always found victims. There never was a man who had greater power in asserting, or who with greater oaths would affirm a thing, yet would observe it less. Nevertheless his deceits always succeeded according to his wishes, since he well understood this side of mankind.
"Nondimanco sempre gli succederono gli inganni (ad votum)." The words "ad votum" are omitted in the Testina edition, 1550.
Alexander never did what he said; Cesare never said what he did.
Italian proverb.

It is unnecessary, then, for a prince to have all the good qualities enumerated; but it is very necessary to appear to have them. I shall dare to say this as well: to have them and always to observe them is harmful; to appear to have them is useful. Appear merciful, faithful, humane, religious, upright — and be so; but with a mind so framed that, should you need not to be so, you are able and know how to change to the opposite.

You must understand that a prince, especially a new one, cannot observe all those things for which men are esteemed, being often compelled, in order to maintain the state, to act contrary to fidelity, friendship, humanity, and religion. He must therefore have a mind ready to turn itself according to the winds and variations of fortune; yet, as said above, not to diverge from the good if he can avoid it, but, if compelled, to know how to take up the opposite course.

"Contrary to fidelity" or "faith" ("contro alla fede"), and "altogether faithful" ("tutto fede") in the next paragraph. It is noteworthy that these two phrases, "contro alla fede" and "tutto fede," were omitted in the Testina edition, published with papal sanction. The meaning attached to "fede" may have been "the faith" — that is, the Catholic creed — rather than "fidelity" as rendered here. Note that "religione" was allowed to stand, being used to signify any shade of belief — as "the religion" was inevitably used to designate the Huguenot heresy. South, in his Sermon IX (p. 69, ed. 1843), comments: "That great patron and Coryphaeus of this tribe, Niccolò Machiavelli, laid down this for a master rule in his political scheme: that the show of religion was helpful to the politician, but the reality of it hurtful and pernicious."

A prince ought to take care that nothing slip from his lips that is not replete with the above-named five qualities, so that he may appear to anyone who sees and hears him altogether merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and religious. There is nothing more necessary to appear to have than this last. Men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand, since it belongs to everyone to see you, to few to come in touch with you. Everyone sees what you appear to be; few really know what you are, and those few dare not oppose themselves to the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state to defend them. In the actions of all men, and especially of princes, which it is not prudent to challenge, one judges by the result.

For this reason, let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state: the means will always be considered honest and he will be praised by everybody. The vulgar are always taken by what a thing appears to be and by what comes of it; and in the world there are only the vulgar, for the few find no place there when the many have no ground to rest on.

One prince of the present time, whom it is not well to name, never preaches anything but peace and good faith — and is most hostile to both; either, if he had kept it, would have deprived him of his reputation or his kingdom many times over.
Ferdinand of Aragon. "When Machiavelli was writing The Prince it would have been clearly impossible to mention Ferdinand's name here without giving offense." — Burd's Il Principe, p. 308.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — Avoiding Being Despised and Hated
paragraphs: Concerning the characteristics mentioned above, I have spoken of the more important ones. The others I wish to discuss briefly under this general heading: the prince must consider how to avoid the things that make him hated or contemptible, as I have in part said before. As often as he succeeds at this, he will have done his part, and need not fear danger from any other reproaches.

It makes him hated above all things, as said, to be rapacious and a violator of the property and women of his subjects — both of which he must abstain from. When their property and honor are not touched, the majority of men live content, and he has only to contend with the ambition of a few, which he can curb with ease in many ways.

It makes him contemptible to be considered fickle, frivolous, effeminate, mean-spirited, or irresolute. From all of these a prince should guard himself as from a rock; he should endeavor to show in his actions greatness, courage, gravity, and fortitude. In his private dealings with his subjects, let him show that his judgments are irrevocable, and maintain himself in such reputation that no one can hope to deceive him or get around him.

A prince who conveys this impression of himself is highly esteemed, and one highly esteemed is not easily conspired against; provided it is well known that he is an excellent man revered by his people, he can only be attacked with difficulty. A prince should have two fears: one internal, from his subjects; the other external, from foreign powers. From the latter he is defended by being well armed and having good allies; if he is well armed he will have good friends, and affairs will remain quiet at home when they are quiet abroad, unless already disturbed by conspiracy. Even if affairs outside are disturbed, so long as he has carried out his preparations and lived as I have said, he will resist every attack as long as he does not despair — as Nabis the Spartan did.

Concerning his subjects, when affairs outside are disturbed he has only to fear secret conspiracy. From this a prince can easily secure himself by avoiding being hated and despised, and by keeping the people satisfied — which he must accomplish above all, as I said at length. One of the most effective remedies against conspiracies is not to be hated and despised by the people; he who conspires against a prince always expects to please them by his removal, but when the conspirator can only expect to offend them, he will not have the courage to undertake it. The difficulties confronting a conspirator are infinite. As experience shows, there have been many conspiracies but few successful ones. He who conspires cannot act alone, nor can he take a companion except from those he believes to be malcontents; and as soon as you open your mind to a malcontent, you give him the material with which to content himself — by denouncing you, he can look for every advantage. Seeing the gain from denunciation as assured, and the other course doubtful and full of dangers, he must be a very rare friend, or a thoroughly obstinate enemy of the prince, to keep faith with you.

To put it briefly: on the conspirator's side there is nothing but fear, jealousy, and prospect of punishment to terrify him; on the prince's side there is the majesty of the principality, the laws, the protection of friends and the state. Add to these popular goodwill, and it becomes impossible for anyone to be rash enough to conspire. A conspirator generally has cause to fear before the execution of his plot; in this case he has also to fear the sequel, since by his deed he makes the people his enemy, and cannot hope for any escape.

Endless examples could be given, but I will be content with one from within our fathers' memory. Messer Annibale Bentivogli, Prince of Bologna (grandfather of the present Annibale), was murdered by the Canneschi, who had conspired against him. Not one of his family survived but Messer Giovanni, still a child. Immediately after the assassination, the people rose and murdered all the Canneschi. This sprang from the popular goodwill the house of Bentivogli enjoyed in Bologna at that time — so great that, though none of the family remained there able to rule, the Bolognese, hearing that a Bentivogli in Florence had until then been considered the son of a blacksmith, sent for him and gave him the government of the city, which he ruled until Messer Giovanni came in due course to govern.

Giovanni Bentivogli, born in Bologna 1438, died in Milan 1508. He ruled Bologna from 1462 to 1506. Machiavelli's strong condemnation of conspiracies may get its edge from his own very recent experience (February 1513), when he was arrested and tortured for alleged complicity in the Boscoli conspiracy.

For this reason I hold that a prince ought to reckon conspiracies of little account when his people hold him in esteem; but when it is hostile and bears hatred toward him, he ought to fear everything and everybody. Well-ordered states and wise princes have taken every care not to drive the nobles to desperation, and to keep the people satisfied and contented; this is one of the most important objects a prince can have.

Among the best-ordered and governed kingdoms of our times is France, and in it are found many good institutions on which the king's liberty and security depend. The first is the parliament and its authority. He who founded the kingdom, knowing the ambition and boldness of the nobility, considered that a bit in their mouths would be necessary to hold them in. On the other hand, knowing the hatred of the people — grounded in fear — against the nobles, he wished to protect them; but he did not want this to be the king's special care. So, to spare himself the reproach either of favoring the people (from the nobles) or of favoring the nobles (from the people), he set up an arbiter to beat down the great and favor the lesser without reproach to the king. There could not be a better or more prudent arrangement, or a greater source of security for king and kingdom. From this we may draw another important conclusion: princes ought to leave affairs of reproach to others to manage, and keep those of grace in their own hands. Further, a prince should cherish the nobles, but not so as to make himself hated by the people.

Some who have examined the lives and deaths of Roman emperors may suppose many of them to be counterexamples, since some of them lived nobly and showed great qualities of soul, yet lost their empire or were killed by conspiring subjects. To answer these objections, I will recall the characters of some emperors and show that the causes of their ruin were not different from what I have alleged. I will submit only what is noteworthy to someone studying the affairs of those times.

It seems sufficient to take all the emperors who succeeded to the empire from Marcus the philosopher down to Maximinus: namely, Marcus and his son Commodus, Pertinax, Julian, Severus and his son Antoninus Caracalla, Macrinus, Heliogabalus, Alexander, and Maximinus.

Note first that, while in other principalities one has only to contend with the ambition of the nobles and the insolence of the people, Roman emperors had a third difficulty: putting up with the cruelty and avarice of their soldiers — a matter so beset with difficulties that it was the ruin of many. It was a hard thing to give satisfaction to both soldiers and people: the people loved peace, and so loved the unaspiring prince; the soldiers loved the warlike prince, bold, cruel, and rapacious — qualities they were quite willing he should exercise on the people, so they could get double pay and give vent to their own greed and cruelty. Hence those emperors were always overthrown who, by birth or training, had no great authority. Most of them, especially those new to the principality, recognizing the difficulty of these two opposing humors, inclined to satisfy the soldiers, caring little about injuring the people. This course was necessary, because, as princes cannot help being hated by someone, they ought first to avoid being hated by everyone; failing that, they should endeavor to avoid the hatred of the most powerful. So those emperors who through inexperience needed special favor adhered more readily to the soldiers than to the people — a course that turned out advantageously or not, according to whether the prince knew how to maintain authority over them.

From these causes it came about that Marcus, Pertinax, and Alexander — all men of modest life, lovers of justice, enemies of cruelty, humane and kindly — came to a sad end, except Marcus. He alone lived and died honored, because he had succeeded to the throne by hereditary title and owed nothing to either soldiers or people. Afterwards, possessed of many virtues that made him respected, he always kept both orders in their places while he lived, and was neither hated nor despised.

Pertinax was made emperor against the wishes of the soldiers, who, accustomed to live licentiously under Commodus, could not endure the honest life to which Pertinax wished to reduce them. Having given cause for hatred, with contempt for his old age added to it, he was overthrown at the very beginning of his administration. Here it should be noted that hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones; therefore, as I said before, a prince wishing to keep his state is very often forced to do evil. When the body whose help you need to maintain yourself — whether people, soldiers, or nobles — is corrupt, you must submit to its humors and gratify them, and then good works will do you harm.

Let us come to Alexander, who was a man of such great goodness that among the praises accorded him is this: in the fourteen years he held the empire, no one was ever put to death by him unjudged. Nevertheless, being considered effeminate and a man who allowed himself to be governed by his mother, he became despised; the army conspired against him and murdered him.

Turning now to the opposite characters — Commodus, Severus, Antoninus Caracalla, and Maximinus — you will find them all cruel and rapacious, men who to satisfy their soldiers did not hesitate to commit every kind of iniquity against the people. All except Severus came to a bad end. In Severus there was so much valor that, keeping the soldiers friendly though the people were oppressed by him, he reigned successfully. His valor made him so admired in the sight of soldiers and people that the latter were kept somewhat astonished and awed, and the former respectful and satisfied. Because this man's actions as a new prince were great, I wish to show briefly that he knew well how to counterfeit both the fox and the lion — natures which, as said above, a prince must know how to imitate.

Knowing the sloth of the Emperor Julian, Severus persuaded the army in Slavonia (of which he was captain) that it would be right to go to Rome and avenge the death of Pertinax, who had been killed by the praetorian soldiers. Under this pretext, without appearing to aspire to the throne, he moved the army on Rome and reached Italy before it was known he had started. On his arrival at Rome, the Senate, through fear, elected him emperor and killed Julian. After this there remained for Severus two difficulties, wishing to master the whole empire: one in Asia, where Niger, head of the Asian army, had had himself proclaimed emperor; the other in the west, where Albinus also aspired to the throne. Considering it dangerous to declare himself hostile to both, he decided to attack Niger and deceive Albinus. To Albinus he wrote that, having been elected emperor by the Senate, he wished to share that dignity with him, and sent him the title of Caesar; moreover, that the Senate had made Albinus his colleague. These things Albinus accepted as true. But after Severus had conquered and killed Niger and settled oriental affairs, he returned to Rome and complained to the Senate that Albinus, little recognizing the benefits received from him, had treacherously sought to murder him, and for this ingratitude he was compelled to punish him. Afterwards he sought him out in France and took from him his government and his life. He who carefully examines this man's actions will find him a most valiant lion and a most cunning fox; he will find him feared and respected by everyone, not hated by the army. It need not be wondered at that he, a new man, was able to hold the empire so well — his supreme renown always protected him from the hatred the people might have conceived against him for his violence.

His son Antoninus was a most eminent man with excellent qualities that made him admirable in the sight of the people and acceptable to the soldiers — he was warlike, most enduring of fatigue, a despiser of delicate food and other luxuries, which made him beloved by the armies. Nevertheless, his ferocity and cruelty were so great and unheard of that, after endless individual murders, he killed a large part of the people of Rome and all those of Alexandria. He became hated by the whole world, and also feared by those around him, to such an extent that he was murdered in the midst of his army by a centurion. Note that such deaths — deliberately inflicted with a resolved and desperate courage — cannot be avoided by princes; anyone who does not fear death can inflict them. But a prince may fear them the less, because they are very rare; he need only be careful not to do any grave injury to those he employs or has around him in the service of the state. Antoninus had not taken this care: he had contumeliously killed the brother of that centurion, and daily threatened him, yet kept him in his bodyguard. This was, as it turned out, a rash thing to do, and it proved the emperor's ruin.

Let us come to Commodus, to whom it should have been very easy to hold the empire, since being Marcus's son he had inherited it, and had only to follow in his father's footsteps to please both people and soldiers. But being by nature cruel and brutal, he gave himself up to amusing and corrupting the soldiers so he could indulge his rapacity upon the people. On the other hand, not maintaining his dignity — often descending into the theater to compete with gladiators and doing other vile things little worthy of imperial majesty — he fell into contempt with the soldiers. Being hated by one party and despised by the other, he was conspired against and killed.

It remains to discuss the character of Maximinus. A very warlike man, he was elected to the throne by armies disgusted with the effeminacy of Alexander, whom they killed. He did not possess the throne long. Two things made him hated and despised: first, his having kept sheep in Thrace, which brought him into contempt (well known to all, and considered a great indignity by everyone); second, his having at his accession deferred going to Rome and taking possession of the imperial seat. He had also gained a reputation for the utmost ferocity, having practiced many cruelties through his prefects in Rome and elsewhere, so that the whole world was moved to anger at the meanness of his birth and to fear at his barbarity. First Africa rebelled; then the Senate with all the people of Rome; then all Italy conspired against him. Add his own army: besieging Aquileia and meeting difficulties taking it, disgusted with his cruelties, and fearing him less when they found so many against him, they murdered him.

I do not wish to discuss Heliogabalus, Macrinus, or Julian, who, being thoroughly contemptible, were quickly wiped out. I will bring this discourse to a close by saying that princes in our times have this difficulty of giving inordinate satisfaction to their soldiers to a much lesser degree. Though one has to give them some indulgence, it is soon done: none of these princes have armies that are veterans in the governance and administration of provinces, as the armies of the Roman Empire were. Whereas it was then more necessary to give satisfaction to the soldiers than to the people, now it is more necessary for all princes, except the Turk and the Soldan, to satisfy the people rather than the soldiers — because the people are the more powerful.

I have excepted the Turk, who always keeps around him twelve thousand infantry and fifteen thousand cavalry on whom the security and strength of the kingdom depend; he must, putting aside every consideration for the people, keep these his friends. The Soldan's kingdom is similar; being entirely in the hands of soldiers, he too must, without regard to the people, keep the soldiers his friends. Note that the Soldan's state is unlike all other principalities, in that it resembles the Christian papacy, which cannot be called either hereditary or newly formed: the old prince's sons are not heirs, but he who is elected by those with authority, and the sons remain only noblemen. This being an ancient custom, it cannot be called a new principality, since it has none of the difficulties met with in new ones: though the prince is new, the constitution of the state is old, framed to receive him as if he were its hereditary lord.

Returning to our subject: anyone who considers it will admit that either hatred or contempt has been fatal to the above-named emperors. It will also be recognized how, some of them acting one way and some another, only one in each group came to a happy end, the rest to unhappy ones. It would have been useless and dangerous for Pertinax and Alexander, being new princes, to imitate Marcus, who was heir to the principality; likewise it would have been utterly destructive for Caracalla, Commodus, and Maximinus to have imitated Severus, not having sufficient valor to follow in his footsteps. A prince new to the principality, then, cannot imitate the actions of Marcus, nor, again, is it necessary to follow those of Severus; but he ought to take from Severus those parts necessary for founding his state, and from Marcus those proper and glorious for keeping a state already stable and firm.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — Are Fortresses and Other Defenses Advantageous or Harmful?
paragraphs: 1. Some princes, to hold the state securely, have disarmed their subjects; others have kept their subject towns distracted by factions; others have fostered enmities against themselves; others have exerted themselves to win over those they distrusted at the beginning of their rule; some have built fortresses; some have demolished them. One cannot give a final judgment on all these things without possessing the particulars of the states in which the decision has to be made, but I will speak as comprehensively as the matter itself will allow.

2. There never was a new prince who disarmed his subjects; on the contrary, finding them disarmed he has always armed them. By arming them, those arms become yours; those men who were distrusted become faithful; those who were faithful are kept so; and your subjects become your adherents. Since not all subjects can be armed, when those you do arm are benefited, the others can be handled more freely; this difference in treatment, which they fully understand, makes the first group your dependents, and the latter group — holding that those who face more danger and service should have the most reward — excuse you. But when you disarm them, you at once offend them, showing that you distrust them either for cowardice or disloyalty; either view breeds hatred against you. And since you cannot remain unarmed, you must turn to mercenaries, whose character has been shown already; even if they were good, they would not be enough to defend you against powerful enemies and distrusted subjects. So, as I said, a new prince in a new principality has always distributed arms. Histories are full of examples. But when a prince acquires a new state that he adds as a province to his old one, he must disarm the men of that state, except those who were his adherents in acquiring it; and these in turn, with time and opportunity, should be rendered soft and effeminate. Things should be arranged so that all the armed men in the state shall be your own soldiers who lived near you in your old state.

3. Our forefathers, considered wise, used to say it was necessary to hold Pistoia by factions and Pisa by fortresses; with this idea they fostered quarrels in some tributary towns to keep them more easily. This may have been well enough when Italy was somehow balanced, but I do not believe it can be accepted as a precept today. I do not believe factions can ever be of use; on the contrary, when the enemy comes upon you in divided cities, you are quickly lost, because the weakest party will always assist the outside forces, and the other will not be able to resist. The Venetians, moved, I believe, by the above reasoning, fostered the Guelph and Ghibelline factions in their tributary cities; though they never allowed them to come to bloodshed, they nursed these disputes so that the citizens, distracted by their differences, would not unite against them. As we saw, this did not afterwards turn out as expected: after the rout at Vailà, one party at once took courage and seized the state. Such methods argue weakness in the prince; factions will never be permitted in a vigorous principality. Such methods are useful only in times of peace, for managing subjects more easily; but when war comes, the policy proves fallacious.

4. Without doubt princes become great by overcoming difficulties and obstacles; and therefore fortune, especially when she wishes to make a new prince great — he having a greater need to earn renown than a hereditary prince — causes enemies to rise and form designs against him, so that he may have the opportunity of overcoming them, and rise higher by them as by a ladder which his enemies have raised. For this reason many hold that a wise prince, when he has the opportunity, ought with craft to foster some animosity against himself, so that, having crushed it, his renown may rise higher.

5. Princes, especially new ones, have found more fidelity and help in those who, at the beginning of their rule, were distrusted than in those who were trusted. Pandolfo Petrucci, Prince of Siena, ruled his state more by those who had been distrusted than by others. On this, however, one cannot generalize; it varies so much with the individual. I will only say this: those men who at the start of a princedom were hostile, if they need support, can always be won over with the greatest ease; they will serve the prince with the closer fidelity because they know they must cancel by deeds the bad impression he had of them. Thus the prince always gets more profit from them than from those who, serving him in too much security, may neglect his affairs. Since the matter calls for it, I must warn a prince who by means of secret favors has acquired a new state: he must carefully consider the reasons that induced those who favored him to do so. If it is not natural affection for him but mere discontent with their previous government, then he will keep them friendly only with great trouble and difficulty — it will be impossible to satisfy them. Weighing the reasons in examples from ancient and modern affairs, we shall find it easier for the prince to make friends of men who were content under the former government (and therefore his enemies) than of those who, being discontented with it, favored him and encouraged him to seize it.

6. It has been customary for princes, to hold their states more securely, to build fortresses as a bridle and bit for those who might design against them, and as a place of refuge from a first attack. I praise this system because it has been used before. Nevertheless, in our times Messer Niccolò Vitelli has been seen to demolish two fortresses in Città di Castello to hold that state; Guido Ubaldo, Duke of Urbino, on returning to his dominion, having been driven out by Cesare Borgia, razed to the foundations all fortresses in the province, considering that without them the dominion would be harder to lose; the Bentivogli on returning to Bologna came to a similar decision. Fortresses, then, are useful or not according to circumstances; if they do you good in one way, they injure you in another. This question may be reasoned thus: the prince with more to fear from the people than from foreigners ought to build fortresses; he with more to fear from foreigners than from the people ought to leave them alone. The Castle of Milan, built by Francesco Sforza, has made, and will make, more trouble for the house of Sforza than any other disorder in the state. For this reason the best possible fortress is not to be hated by the people: even if you hold the fortresses, they will not save you if the people hate you — foreigners will never be lacking to assist a people who have taken arms against you. In our times we have not seen fortresses of use to any prince except the Countess of Forlì, when Count Girolamo, her consort, was killed; by means of her fortresses she was able to withstand the popular attack and wait for assistance from Milan, and thus recover her state; the posture of affairs at the time was such that foreigners could not assist the people. But fortresses were of little use to her afterwards, when Cesare Borgia attacked her, and when the people — her enemy — were allied with foreigners. It would have been safer for her, both then and before, not to have been hated by the people than to have had the fortresses. All things considered, then, I shall praise him who builds fortresses as well as him who does not, and blame whoever, trusting in them, cares little about being hated by the people.

Catherine Sforza, daughter of Galeazzo Sforza and Lucrezia Landriani, born 1463, died 1509. It was to the Countess of Forlì that Machiavelli was sent as envoy in 1499. A letter from Fortunati to the countess announces the appointment: "I have been with the signori to learn whom they would send and when. They tell me that Niccolò Machiavelli, a learned young Florentine noble, secretary to my Lords of the Ten, is to leave with me at once." Cf. "Catherine Sforza," by Count Pasolini, translated by P. Sylvester, 1898.

chapters.title: Chapter 21 — How a Prince Should Conduct Himself to Gain Renown
paragraphs: Nothing makes a prince so much esteemed as great enterprises and setting a fine example. In our time we have Ferdinand of Aragon, the present King of Spain. He can almost be called a new prince, since by fame and glory he has risen from being an insignificant king to the foremost king in Christendom. If you consider his deeds, you will find them all great, some of them extraordinary. At the beginning of his reign he attacked Granada, and this enterprise laid the foundation of his dominions. He did this quietly at first, without fear of hindrance: he kept the minds of the barons of Castile occupied with thinking of the war, not anticipating any innovations, so they did not perceive that by these means he was acquiring power and authority over them. He was able with the money of the Church and of the people to sustain his armies, and by that long war to lay the foundation of the military skill that has since distinguished him. Further, always using religion as a plea in order to undertake greater schemes, he devoted himself with pious cruelty to driving out and clearing his kingdom of the Moors; there could be no more admirable example, nor any rarer. Under this same cloak he assailed Africa, came down into Italy, and finally attacked France. His achievements and designs have always been great, keeping the minds of his people in suspense and admiration, occupied with the outcome. His actions have arisen one out of the other in such a way that men have never been given time to work steadily against him.

It also greatly helps a prince to set unusual examples in internal affairs, such as those related of Messer Bernabò of Milan, who, when he had the chance — whenever someone in civil life did something extraordinary, good or bad — would use some method of rewarding or punishing him that would be much talked about. Above all things, a prince should always endeavor in every action to gain the reputation of being a great and remarkable man.

A prince is also respected when he is either a true friend or a downright enemy — that is, when, without any reservation, he declares himself in favor of one party against the other. This course will always be more advantageous than standing neutral. If two of your powerful neighbors come to blows, they are such that if one of them conquers, you either have to fear him or not. In either case it will always be more advantageous to declare yourself and wage war strenuously. In the first case, if you do not declare yourself, you will invariably fall prey to the conqueror, to the pleasure and satisfaction of the one conquered, and you will have no reasons to offer, nothing to protect or shelter you. The conqueror does not want doubtful friends who will not aid him in the time of trial; the loser will not harbor you, because you did not willingly, sword in hand, court his fate.

Antiochus went into Greece, sent for by the Aetolians to drive out the Romans. He sent envoys to the Achaeans (friends of the Romans), urging them to remain neutral; the Romans urged them to take up arms. The question came up in the council of the Achaeans, where Antiochus's legate urged neutrality. The Roman legate answered: "As for what has been said, that it is better and more advantageous for your state not to interfere in our war, nothing could be more erroneous; by not interfering you will be left, without favor or consideration, the prize of the conqueror." Thus it will always happen: he who is not your friend will demand your neutrality, while he who is your friend will urge you to declare yourself with arms. Irresolute princes, to avoid present dangers, generally follow the neutral path, and are generally ruined. But when a prince declares himself gallantly in favor of one side, if that side wins — though the victor may be powerful and have him at his mercy — he is indebted to him, and a bond of friendship is formed. Men are never so shameless as to become a monument of ingratitude by oppressing you. Victories are never so complete that the victor need not show some regard, especially for justice. And if the side you join loses, he may shelter you, and while he can, he may aid you, and you become companions on a fortune that may rise again.

In the second case, when those who fight are such that you have no anxiety about who may conquer, it is all the more prudent to ally: you assist at the destruction of one by the aid of another who, had he been wise, would have saved him; and by conquering — as he cannot fail to do with your assistance — he remains at your discretion. Note that a prince ought to take care never to make an alliance with one more powerful than himself for attacking others, unless necessity compels him. If he conquers, you are at his discretion, and princes ought to avoid as much as possible being at anyone's discretion. The Venetians joined with France against the Duke of Milan, and this alliance, which caused their ruin, could have been avoided. But when it cannot be avoided, as happened to the Florentines when the Pope and Spain sent armies to attack Lombardy, then, for the reasons given, the prince ought to favor one of the parties.

Never let any government imagine that it can choose perfectly safe courses; rather, let it expect to have to take very doubtful ones. In ordinary affairs, one never seeks to avoid one trouble without running into another; prudence consists in knowing how to distinguish the character of troubles, and to take the lesser evil.

A prince ought also to show himself a patron of ability, and to honor the proficient in every art. At the same time he should encourage his citizens to practice their callings peaceably, in commerce, agriculture, and every other pursuit — so that one is not deterred from improving his possessions for fear they will be taken away, and another from opening up trade for fear of taxes. Rather, the prince ought to offer rewards to whoever wishes to do these things and designs in any way to honor his city or state.

Further, he ought to entertain the people with festivals and spectacles at convenient seasons. Since every city is divided into guilds or societies, he ought to hold such bodies in esteem, associate with them sometimes, and show himself an example of courtesy and liberality — always, however, maintaining the majesty of his rank, which he must never consent to abate in anything.

"Guilds or societies": "in arti o in tribù." "Arti" were craft or trade guilds; cf. Florio: "Arte… a whole company of any trade in any city or corporation town." The guilds of Florence are admirably described by Mr. Edgcumbe Staley (Methuen, 1906). Similar institutions, called "artel," exist in Russia today (cf. Sir Mackenzie Wallace's Russia, ed. 1905: "The sons… were always during the working season members of an artel. In some larger towns there are artels of a much more complex kind — permanent associations, possessing large capital, and pecuniarily responsible for the acts of individual members"). Despite the apparent similarity, "artel" (Mr. Aylmer Maude assures me) has no connection with "ars" or "arte"; its root is that of the verb "rotitsya," to bind oneself by an oath, and it is generally admitted to be only another form of "rota," now signifying a "regimental company." In both words the underlying idea is a body of men united by an oath. "Tribù" were possibly gentile groups united by common descent, including individuals connected by marriage. "Sects" or "clans" would perhaps be the most appropriate English equivalent.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 — The Secretaries of Princes
paragraphs: The choice of servants is of no little importance to a prince; they are good or not according to the prince's discrimination. The first opinion one forms of a prince, and of his understanding, is by observing the men around him. When they are capable and faithful, he may always be considered wise, since he has known how to recognize the capable and keep them faithful. When they are otherwise, one cannot form a good opinion of him — the prime error he made was in choosing them.

No one who knew Messer Antonio da Venafro as the servant of Pandolfo Petrucci, Prince of Siena, would fail to consider Pandolfo a very clever man for having Venafro as his servant. There are three classes of intellects: one that comprehends by itself; another that appreciates what others have comprehended; and a third that neither comprehends by itself nor by the showing of others. The first is most excellent, the second good, the third useless. It follows that if Pandolfo was not in the first rank, he was in the second. Whenever a man has the judgment to know good and bad when it is said and done, even if he has not the initiative himself, he can still recognize good and bad in his servant — praising the one, correcting the other — and so the servant cannot hope to deceive him, and is kept honest.

To enable a prince to form an opinion of his servant, there is one test that never fails: when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours, and seeking inwardly his own profit in everything, such a man will never make a good servant, nor will you ever be able to trust him. He who has the state of another in his hands ought never to think of himself, but always of his prince, and never pay attention to matters in which the prince is not concerned.

On the other hand, to keep his servant honest, the prince ought to study him — honoring him, enriching him, doing him kindnesses, sharing with him the honors and cares. At the same time he should let the servant see he cannot stand alone, so that many honors may not make him want more, many riches make him want more, and many cares make him dread chance. When servants, and princes toward servants, are thus disposed, they can trust each other; when otherwise, the end will always be disastrous for one or the other.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 — How Flatterers Should Be Avoided
paragraphs: I do not wish to leave out an important branch of this subject, for it is a danger from which princes are with difficulty preserved unless they are very careful and discriminating. It is that of flatterers, of whom courts are full. Men are so self-complacent in their own affairs, and so deceived in them, that they are preserved with difficulty from this pest; and if they wish to defend themselves, they run the danger of falling into contempt. There is no other way of guarding against flatterers than by letting men understand that telling you the truth will not offend you — but when everyone may tell you the truth, respect for you abates.

A wise prince ought therefore to take a third course: choose the wise men in his state and give them alone the liberty of speaking the truth to him, and only about things he asks about, not others. But he ought to question them on everything, listen to their opinions, and afterwards form his own conclusions. With these counselors, separately and collectively, he ought to bear himself in such a way that each knows that the more freely he speaks, the more he will be preferred. Outside these, he should listen to no one, pursue the thing resolved on, and be steadfast in his resolutions. He who does otherwise is either overthrown by flatterers, or so often changed by varying opinions that he falls into contempt.

On this subject I wish to give a modern example. Fra Luca, man of affairs to Maximilian the present emperor, speaking of his majesty, said: he consulted with no one, yet never got his own way in anything. This arose from his following the opposite of the practice described: the emperor is a secretive man — he does not communicate his designs to anyone, nor does he receive opinions on them. But since, in carrying them out, they become revealed and known, they are at once obstructed by the men around him; he, being pliant, is diverted from them. Hence what he does one day he undoes the next; no one ever understands what he wishes or intends to do, and no one can rely on his resolutions.
Maximilian I, born 1459, died 1519, Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire. He married first Mary, daughter of Charles the Bold; after her death, Bianca Sforza, thus becoming involved in Italian politics.

A prince ought, then, always to take counsel — but only when he wishes, not when others wish. He ought rather to discourage everyone from offering advice unless he asks for it. But he should be a constant inquirer, and afterwards a patient listener about the things he has asked about. Also, on learning that anyone has not told him the truth for whatever reason, he should let his anger be felt.

If some think that a prince who gives an impression of wisdom is not wise through his own ability but through the good advisers around him, they are certainly deceived. This is an axiom that never fails: a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice, unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person who happens to be very prudent. In that case he may indeed be well governed, but not for long — such a governor would in a short time take his state from him.

But a prince who is not inexperienced and takes counsel from more than one will never get united counsel, nor will he know how to unite the counsel he receives. Each counselor will think of his own interests, and the prince will not know how to control them or see through them. They are not to be found otherwise: men will always prove untrue to you unless kept honest by constraint. So we must conclude that good counsels, wherever they come from, are born of the prince's wisdom, not the prince's wisdom from good counsels.

chapters.title: Chapter 24 — Why the Princes of Italy Have Lost Their States
paragraphs: The previous suggestions, carefully observed, will enable a new prince to appear well established, and render him at once more secure and fixed in the state than if he had long been seated there. The actions of a new prince are more narrowly observed than those of a hereditary one; when they are seen to be able, they gain him more men and bind far tighter than ancient blood. Men are attracted more by the present than by the past; when they find the present good, they enjoy it and seek no further. They will also make the utmost defense of a prince if he does not fail them in other things. It will thus be a double glory for him to have established a new principality and adorned and strengthened it with good laws, good arms, good allies, and a good example; so too it is a double disgrace to one who, born a prince, loses his state through want of wisdom.

And if one considers the lords who have lost their states in Italy in our times — the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and others — there will be found in them first a common defect in arms, from the causes discussed at length; next, one or another of them will be seen either to have had the people hostile, or, if he had the people friendly, to have failed to secure the nobles. Without these defects, states that have power enough to keep an army in the field cannot be lost.

Philip of Macedon — not the father of Alexander the Great, but the one conquered by Titus Quintius — had not much territory compared with the greatness of the Romans and Greece who attacked him. Yet being a warlike man who knew how to attract the people and secure the nobles, he sustained the war against his enemies for many years; and if at the end he lost the dominion of some cities, he still retained the kingdom.

Let not our princes, then, accuse fortune for the loss of their principalities after so many years' possession, but rather their own sloth. In quiet times they never thought there could be a change — it is a common defect of man not to make any provision in calm for the tempest. When the bad times came, they thought of flight, not of defending themselves, and hoped the people, disgusted with the insolence of the conquerors, would recall them. This course, when others fail, may be good; but it is very bad to have neglected all other expedients for its sake. You would never wish to fall because you trusted to find someone later to restore you. Either this does not happen, or, if it does, it will not be for your security; for that deliverance is of no value which does not depend upon yourself. Only those means are reliable, certain, and durable that depend upon yourself and your own valor.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 — What Fortune Can Effect in Human Affairs
paragraphs: I am not unaware that many have had, and still have, the opinion that the affairs of the world are so governed by fortune and by God that men with their wisdom cannot direct them and no one can even help them; from this they would have us conclude that it is not necessary to labor much in affairs, but to let chance govern them. This opinion has been more credited in our times because of the great changes in affairs that have been seen, and may still be seen, every day, beyond all human conjecture. Sometimes, pondering this, I am to some degree inclined to their opinion. Still, not to extinguish our free will, I hold it to be true that fortune is the arbiter of one half of our actions, but that she leaves us to direct the other half, or perhaps a little less.

Frederick the Great used to say: "The older one gets, the more convinced one becomes that His Majesty King Chance does three-quarters of the business of this miserable universe." — Sorel's Eastern Question.

I compare fortune to one of those raging rivers that, when in flood, overflows the plains, sweeping away trees and buildings, bearing away the soil from place to place. Everything flies before it; all yield to its violence, unable to withstand it. Yet, though its nature is such, it does not follow that men, when the weather is fair, shall not make provision with defenses and barriers — so that when the river rises again, the waters may pass away by canal, and their force may be neither so unrestrained nor so dangerous. So it happens with fortune: she shows her power where valor has not prepared to resist her, and turns her forces where she knows barriers and defenses have not been raised to constrain her.

Consider Italy, the seat of these changes and the source of their impulse: you will see it is an open country without barriers and without any defense. Had it been defended by proper valor, as are Germany, Spain, and France, either the invasion would not have made the great changes it has, or it would not have come at all. This I consider enough to say about resistance to fortune in general.

Coming to the particular: a prince may be seen happy today and ruined tomorrow without having shown any change of disposition or character. This arises, I believe, first from causes discussed at length — namely, that the prince who relies entirely on fortune is lost when it changes. I also believe that he will be successful who directs his actions according to the spirit of the times, and that he whose actions do not accord with the times will not be successful. Men, in affairs leading to the end every man has before him (glory and riches), are seen to get there by various methods: one with caution, another with haste; one by force, another by skill; one by patience, another by its opposite. Each succeeds in reaching the goal by a different method. One can also see of two cautious men that one attains his end and the other fails; and two men by different methods equally succeed, one cautious, the other impetuous. All this arises from nothing other than whether or not they conform in their methods to the spirit of the times. From this it follows that two men working differently may bring about the same effect, and two working similarly — one attains his object and the other does not.

Changes of estate also issue from this. If, for one who governs himself with caution and patience, the times and affairs converge so that his administration succeeds, his fortune is made; but if times and affairs change, he is ruined unless he changes his course. But a man is not often found sufficiently circumspect to accommodate himself to the change: partly because he cannot deviate from what nature inclines him to do, and partly because, having always prospered by acting in one way, he cannot be persuaded to leave it. The cautious man, when it is time to turn adventurous, does not know how; and so he is ruined. Had he changed his conduct with the times, fortune would not have changed.

Pope Julius II went to work impetuously in all his affairs, and found the times and circumstances so well in accord with that line of action that he always met with success. Consider his first enterprise against Bologna, while Messer Giovanni Bentivogli was still alive. The Venetians were not agreeable, nor was the King of Spain, and he had the enterprise still under discussion with the King of France. Nevertheless, he personally entered upon the expedition with his accustomed boldness and energy — a move that made Spain and the Venetians stand irresolute and passive, the latter from fear, the former from their desire to recover the Kingdom of Naples. On the other hand, he drew after him the King of France, who, observing the movement and desiring to make the Pope his friend so as to humble the Venetians, found it impossible to refuse him. Julius, by his impetuous action, accomplished what no other pontiff could have done with simple human wisdom. If he had waited in Rome until he could leave with his plans arranged and everything fixed, as another pontiff would, he would never have succeeded; the King of France would have made a thousand excuses, and the others would have raised a thousand fears.

I will leave his other actions aside: they were all alike and all succeeded, the shortness of his life not letting him experience the contrary. But if circumstances had arisen that required caution, his ruin would have followed — he would never have deviated from those ways to which nature inclined him.

I conclude, then, that fortune being changeful and men steadfast in their ways, so long as the two are in agreement men are successful; unsuccessful when they fall out. For my part, I hold it better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under control, it is necessary to beat and coerce her. It is seen that she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who proceed coldly. She is always, woman-like, a lover of young men, because they are less cautious, more violent, and with more audacity command her.

chapters.title: Chapter 26 — An Exhortation to Liberate Italy from the Barbarians
paragraphs: Having carefully considered the subject of the above discourses, and wondering whether the present times were propitious to a new prince, and whether there were elements that would give a wise and virtuous one the opportunity to introduce a new order of things that would do honor to him and good to the people of this country, it appears to me that so many things concur to favor a new prince that I have never known a time more fit than the present.

If, as I said, it was necessary that the people of Israel be captive to make manifest the ability of Moses; that the Persians be oppressed by the Medes to reveal the greatness of Cyrus's soul; that the Athenians be dispersed to display the capabilities of Theseus — then at the present time, to discover the virtue of an Italian spirit, it was necessary that Italy should be reduced to the extremity she is now in: more enslaved than the Hebrews, more oppressed than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians; without head, without order, beaten, despoiled, torn, overrun; having endured every kind of desolation.
