Though lately some spark may have been shown by one, making us think he was ordained by God for our redemption, it was afterwards seen, at the height of his career, that fortune rejected him. So Italy, left as without life, waits for him who shall heal her wounds and put an end to the ravaging and plundering of Lombardy, to the extortions and taxings of the Kingdom and of Tuscany, and cleanse those sores that have long festered. One sees her entreating God to send someone to deliver her from these wrongs and barbarous insolences. One sees also that she is ready and willing to follow a banner, if only someone will raise it.

Nor is there at present anyone in whom she can place more hope than in your illustrious house, with its valor and fortune, favored by God and by the Church of which it is now the chief, and which could be made the head of this redemption. This will not be difficult if you recall the actions and lives of the men I have named. Although they were great and wonderful, they were men; each had no more opportunity than the present offers. Their enterprises were not more just or easier than this, nor was God more their friend than He is yours.
Giuliano de' Medici. He had just been created a cardinal by Leo X. In 1523 Giuliano was elected Pope, taking the title of Clement VII.

We have great justice on our side, for that war is just which is necessary, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope but in them. Here there is the greatest willingness; and where the willingness is great, the difficulties cannot be great — if you will only follow those men I have directed your attention to. Further, how extraordinarily the ways of God have been manifested, beyond example: the sea is divided, a cloud has led the way, the rock has poured forth water, it has rained manna, everything has contributed to your greatness. You must do the rest. God is not willing to do everything, and thus take away our free will and that share of glory which belongs to us.

It is no wonder that none of the above-named Italians have been able to accomplish what is expected of your illustrious house; in so many revolutions in Italy, and in so many campaigns, it has always appeared that military virtue was exhausted, because the old order of things was not good and none of us have known how to find a new one. Nothing honors a man more than to establish new laws and new ordinances when he himself has newly risen. Such things, well founded and dignified, will make him revered and admired; in Italy there is no lack of opportunities to bring them into use in every form.

Here there is great valor in the limbs, while it fails in the head. Look at the duels and hand-to-hand combats — how superior the Italians are in strength, dexterity, and subtlety. But when it comes to armies, they do not bear comparison. This springs entirely from the insufficiency of the leaders; those who are capable are not obeyed, and each one thinks he knows best, no one being so distinguished above the rest, by valor or fortune, that others would yield to him. For so long a time, and during so much fighting in the past twenty years, whenever there has been an army wholly Italian, it has always given a poor account of itself: witness Il Taro, Alessandria, Capua, Genoa, Vailà, Bologna, Mestri.
The battles of Il Taro, 1495; Alessandria, 1499; Capua, 1501; Genoa, 1507; Vailà, 1509; Bologna, 1511; Mestri, 1513.

If, then, your illustrious house wishes to follow the remarkable men who have redeemed their country, it is necessary, as a true foundation for every enterprise, to be provided with your own forces; there can be no more faithful, truer, or better soldiers. Although singly they are good, altogether they will be much better when commanded by their prince, honored by him, and maintained at his expense. It is necessary, then, to be prepared with such arms, so that you can be defended against foreigners by Italian valor.

Though Swiss and Spanish infantry are considered very formidable, both have defects by reason of which a third order could not only oppose them but be relied on to overthrow them. The Spaniards cannot resist cavalry, and the Swiss are afraid of infantry whenever they meet them in close combat. Hence, as has been seen and may be seen again, Spaniards cannot resist French cavalry, and the Swiss are overthrown by Spanish infantry. Though complete proof of this latter cannot be shown, there was some evidence at the battle of Ravenna, when the Spanish infantry faced German battalions (who follow the same tactics as the Swiss): the Spaniards, by agility of body and with the aid of their shields, got in under the pikes of the Germans and stood out of danger, able to attack, while the Germans stood helpless; if the cavalry had not dashed up, all would have been over with them. Knowing the defects of both infantries, then, it is possible to invent a new one that will resist cavalry and not fear infantry — not by creating a new order of arms, but by a variation on the old. Such improvements confer reputation and power on a new prince.

This opportunity, then, must not be allowed to pass: let Italy at last see her liberator appear. Nor can one express the love with which he would be received in all those provinces that have suffered so much from these foreign scourings — with what thirst for revenge, what stubborn faith, what devotion, what tears. What door would be closed to him? Who would refuse him obedience? What envy would hinder him? What Italian would refuse him homage? To all of us this barbarous dominion stinks. Let, then, your illustrious house take up this charge with the courage and hope with which just enterprises are undertaken, so that under its standard our country may be ennobled, and under its auspices may be verified that saying of Petrarch:
Virtù contro al furore / Prenderà l'arme, e fia il combatter corto: / Che l'antico valore / Negli italici cor non è ancor morto.
Virtue against fury shall advance the fight, / And in the combat soon shall put to flight: / For the old Roman valor is not dead, / Nor in th' Italians' breasts extinguished.
Edward Dacre, 1640.
